title: Extract A: Lasseter’s Lost Reef & Extract B: The Oak Island Mystery
passage:
Extract A: Lasseter’s Lost Reef

In 1897, Harold Bell Lasseter a gold prospector was found unconscious in the desert southwest of Alice Springs by an Afghan camel-driver, with a few curious rocks in his pockets. And the legend grew from there. He said he had stumbled on a fabulously rich gold reef somewhere in the trackless country to the west, but he would not say exactly where. Later, he told officials that a surveyor had tried to help him fix the spot and that his first finding might have been in 1897 or perhaps in the years just before the Great War. The dates shifted, and so did the story, which only added to the mystery.

By 1930, in the teeth of the Depression, he had persuaded backers to send a well-equipped expedition. They left Alice Springs on 21 July with a truck, a six-wheeled Thornycroft, and even an aircraft. Fred Blakeley led; Errol Coote flew the plane. They headed for Ilbilba, an airstrip scratched into the sand and pushed on despite troubles. Eventually a forced landing cost them their aircraft. Out near Mount Leisler, Lasseter announced that they were badly off course. Tempers frayed. Blakeley, exasperated, turned most of the party back. Lasseter would not give up. He went on with a dingo shooter, Paul Johns, and a string of camels. He came back to camp one evening with concealed rock samples and declared he had found his reef, but he would not show Johns where. They quarrelled in the desert. Johns turned for home. Lasseter went on alone with two camels.

Then the desert closed in. The camels bolted. Lasseter’s eyes inflamed with sandy-blight; his strength ebbed. A local Aboriginal group gave him food and shelter, but he could not recover his animals or his bearings. He cached pages and messages—sometimes under the ashes of camp-fires with carved hints to 'dig'—and crawled into a cave by a lonely creek to wait. Weeks passed. In early 1931 he died of hunger and exhaustion, far from any town but not entirely alone.

A search party led by bushman Bob Buck found him that autumn, buried in the Aboriginal manner beneath branches, not far from a tree later marked with his name. Buck gathered Lasseter’s effects from the cave—his diary among them—and brought the sad news out to the stations and the police. The diary told of the bolting camels, the friendly camp, the blindness, and the last attempt to walk toward the great domes on the horizon. In time, Lasseter’s remains were reinterred at Alice Springs.


Extract B: The Oak Island Mystery

Just off the rugged southeast shore of Nova Scotia lies a tiny island fashioned somewhat like a question mark. The shape is appropriate, for little Oak Island is the scene of a baffling whodunit that has defied solution for over two centuries. Here, ever since 1795, not long after pirates prowled the Atlantic coast and left glittering legends of buried gold in their wake, people have been trying to find out what lies at the bottom of a mysterious shaft dubbed, hopefully, the 'Money Pit.'

Using picks and shovels, divining rods and drilling rigs, treasure hunters poured about .5 million into the Money Pit. Despite more than 20 attempts, no one has yet reached bottom: each time a digging crew has seemed close to success, torrents of water have suddenly surged into the shaft to drown their hopes. Although it’s now known that the Money Pit is protected by an ingenious system of man-made flood tunnels that use the sea as a watchdog, no one knows who dug the pit, or why.

The long parade of searchers began one day 200 years ago, when Daniel McGinnis, a 16-year-old from Chester, Nova Scotia, paddled over to uninhabited Oak Island to hunt for game. On a knoll at one end of the island, he noticed an odd depression. Above it, on a sawed-off tree limb, hung an old ship’s block and tackle. McGinnis’s heart raced, for in the nearby port of LaHave, once a lair for pirates preying on New England shipping, he had heard many legends of buried treasure.

One legend makes the pit the hiding place for the plunder of Captain Kidd, who was hanged for piracy in 1701. Other theories favour the booty of Blackbeard and Henry Morgan, both notorious buccaneers; or the French crown jewels that Louis XVI and Marie Antoinette were said to be carrying when they attempted to flee during the French Revolution; or Shakespeare's missing manuscripts. Whatever the pit may contain, few other treasures have been sought so avidly.

questions.passage:
Extract A: Lasseter’s Lost Reef

In 1897, Harold Bell Lasseter a gold prospector was found unconscious in the desert southwest of Alice Springs by an Afghan camel-driver, with a few curious rocks in his pockets. And the legend grew from there. He said he had stumbled on a fabulously rich gold reef somewhere in the trackless country to the west, but he would not say exactly where. Later, he told officials that a surveyor had tried to help him fix the spot and that his first finding might have been in 1897 or perhaps in the years just before the Great War. The dates shifted, and so did the story, which only added to the mystery.

By 1930, in the teeth of the Depression, he had persuaded backers to send a well-equipped expedition. They left Alice Springs on 21 July with a truck, a six-wheeled Thornycroft, and even an aircraft. Fred Blakeley led; Errol Coote flew the plane. They headed for Ilbilba, an airstrip scratched into the sand and pushed on despite troubles. Eventually a forced landing cost them their aircraft. Out near Mount Leisler, Lasseter announced that they were badly off course. Tempers frayed. Blakeley, exasperated, turned most of the party back. Lasseter would not give up. He went on with a dingo shooter, Paul Johns, and a string of camels. He came back to camp one evening with concealed rock samples and declared he had found his reef, but he would not show Johns where. They quarrelled in the desert. Johns turned for home. Lasseter went on alone with two camels.

Then the desert closed in. The camels bolted. Lasseter’s eyes inflamed with sandy-blight; his strength ebbed. A local Aboriginal group gave him food and shelter, but he could not recover his animals or his bearings. He cached pages and messages—sometimes under the ashes of camp-fires with carved hints to 'dig'—and crawled into a cave by a lonely creek to wait. Weeks passed. In early 1931 he died of hunger and exhaustion, far from any town but not entirely alone.

A search party led by bushman Bob Buck found him that autumn, buried in the Aboriginal manner beneath branches, not far from a tree later marked with his name. Buck gathered Lasseter’s effects from the cave—his diary among them—and brought the sad news out to the stations and the police. The diary told of the bolting camels, the friendly camp, the blindness, and the last attempt to walk toward the great domes on the horizon. In time, Lasseter’s remains were reinterred at Alice Springs.


Extract B: The Oak Island Mystery

Just off the rugged southeast shore of Nova Scotia lies a tiny island fashioned somewhat like a question mark. The shape is appropriate, for little Oak Island is the scene of a baffling whodunit that has defied solution for over two centuries. Here, ever since 1795, not long after pirates prowled the Atlantic coast and left glittering legends of buried gold in their wake, people have been trying to find out what lies at the bottom of a mysterious shaft dubbed, hopefully, the 'Money Pit.'

Using picks and shovels, divining rods and drilling rigs, treasure hunters poured about .5 million into the Money Pit. Despite more than 20 attempts, no one has yet reached bottom: each time a digging crew has seemed close to success, torrents of water have suddenly surged into the shaft to drown their hopes. Although it’s now known that the Money Pit is protected by an ingenious system of man-made flood tunnels that use the sea as a watchdog, no one knows who dug the pit, or why.

The long parade of searchers began one day 200 years ago, when Daniel McGinnis, a 16-year-old from Chester, Nova Scotia, paddled over to uninhabited Oak Island to hunt for game. On a knoll at one end of the island, he noticed an odd depression. Above it, on a sawed-off tree limb, hung an old ship’s block and tackle. McGinnis’s heart raced, for in the nearby port of LaHave, once a lair for pirates preying on New England shipping, he had heard many legends of buried treasure.

One legend makes the pit the hiding place for the plunder of Captain Kidd, who was hanged for piracy in 1701. Other theories favour the booty of Blackbeard and Henry Morgan, both notorious buccaneers; or the French crown jewels that Louis XVI and Marie Antoinette were said to be carrying when they attempted to flee during the French Revolution; or Shakespeare's missing manuscripts. Whatever the pit may contain, few other treasures have been sought so avidly.

questions.options: Extract A|Extract B|Both Extracts|Neither Extract

Hating Alison Ashley (PG)
Directed by Geoff Bennett
Screenplay by Christine Madafferi from the novel by Robin Klein
Rated PG
Cinemas Everywhere
Review by Sandra Hall
it's a girls’ world in this comic and colourful adaptation of a-much-loved children's
novel.
It should come as no surprise that Delta Goodrem doesn't convince as a 14-year-old
schoolgirl. Hiding under a Mona Lisa smile and a Goldilocks wig, she looks like a 20-year-
old pop star on the run from the paparazzi.
Not that it matters. The film of Hating Alison Ashley, Robin Klein's much-read children's
novel, has little to do with the real world. It's set in Ockerdom, a place where we patriotic
filmgoers have spent a lot of time lately, thanks to the run of comedies which have been
trying, with raucous relentlessness, to make themselves loveable in the happy-go-lucky
manner of The Castle.
Hating Alison Ashley is not really Alison's story. As Klein's many fans know, its narrator is
Alison's classmate, Erica Yurken (Saskia Burmeister), a talented self-dramatist, who
fancies she's been stranded in the wrong life. Her refined sensibilities, she thinks, are
more suited to some ivy-covered temple of learning than scungy, working-class Barringa
East, where she's been dumped among the delinquents of 9C. Whenever she can, she
escapes to the sick bay, where her impressive list of imaginary ailments has gained her a
reputation as a creative hypochondriac.
And life at home is no better. Although her sweet-natured mum (Tracy Mann) does her
best, Erica can't forgive her for taking up with Lennie (Richard Carter), a truck driver she
met at Parents Without Partners, or for giving her such unbearable siblings. Her chief
torturer is her elder sister, boy-mad Valjoy (Rachael Carpani), whose boots and big hair
are almost as scary as her interest in martial arts.
School improves for Erica with the arrival of Miss Belmont (Jean Kittson), whose fishnet
stockings and gallows humour give her the air of a semi-respectable dominatrix. Miss
Belmont does the previously unthinkable and keeps 9C in order. She also gives Erica high
marks and makes her fee! special - until the arrival of Goodrem's Alison Ashley.
Alison is perfection incarnate. For a minute or two, Erica fancies she has found a kindred
spirit. But Alison proves to be strangely aloof. And, even worse, the quality of her
classwork eclipses Erica's.

Extract A: Excerpt from ‘Brenda is the Night’ by Geoffrey McSkimming
In the great deserts of Egypt, where the hot and golden-grained sands stretch on and on
towards the shimmering, far away ends of the earth, miracles are said still to happen.
Everything out here is wide open and lonely. Nearly all of the desert land is dry, the sand
baked almost rock-hard in places by the sun. Sometimes, if you are travelling through this |
furnace of a place, you might come across an oasis — a small patch where there is a
water-hole, with palm trees and small plants called Lilies of the Nile growing around it.
Here you will find shade, and you will be able to fill your water-bottle and wet your
handkerchief and tie it around your neck to cool yourself. If you find an oasis in the desert,
you will be very lucky, as they are few and most definitely far between.
Not many people live in the desert. Those who do usually travel around a lot, not staying in
the one place for a very long time at all. Sometimes they will camp at an oasis for a few
weeks, but they will always move on, for they are usually fearful of meeting up with a
certain tribe — a tribe which has dwelt under the Egyptian sun for thousands of years. The
people who live out in the desert will do anything to avoid coming into contact with this
tribe (one man, long ago, was said to have glued ibis feathers to his body and a long
curved stick to his mouth, and then stood on one leg in the sand, crowing loudly, just so
the tribe would think he was a bird and maybe leave him alone), and so they keep
constantly on the move.
The reason why everyone avoids this particular tribe has nothing to do with dastardliness,
or with their being murderers or thieves or taxation cheats — because they’re not. Nor do
the tribe members make rude sounds or push people to the ground and sit on them,
actions which would automatically make them disagreeable. As a matter of fact, the tribe is
fairly harmless. As another matter of fact, they're not even human beings. They are, as
everybody who has journeyed through these wide sandy plains and hills knows, one of the
oldest wayfaring groups in all of the African continent: camels.
Extract B: What is a Mirage?
A mirage is an optical illusion. Most commonly observed in desert environments, mirages
arise when the sun-heated ground warms the adjacent layer of air more intensely than
the air above it, producing a steep temperature gradient. Since warmer air is less dense
than cooler air, light traversing these layers undergoes continual refraction—bending
gradually away from regions of lower density.
Travellers crossing arid expanses may glimpse what seems to be a shimmering oasis just
ahead—a patch of glimmering water fringed by palm trees and verdant foliage.
Compelled by thirst and hope, they advance, only to find the vision dissolving as they
approach. In reality, the water and trees lie far beyond the true horizon, their light
refracted upward by the denser, cooler air above the hot surface layer. This type of
mirage, known as an inferior mirage, produces inverted—or “upside-down’—images of
the distant scene directly beneath the upright image, explaining why one might perceive a
waterline or the glint of liquid on the desert floor.
Asimilar process occurs at sea under particular atmospheric conditions, giving rise to
superior mirages, in which cooler air lies closer to the ocean’s surface and warmer air sits
aloft. Light from a ship beyond the horizon can be bent downward into the colder layer,
causing the vessel to appear lifted, elongated or even inverted above its actual position—
sometimes floating eerily above the waterline. Mariners of old recorded such spectral
sightings, attributing them to supernatural forces, yet we now understand them as natural
consequences of atmospheric refraction.

This article comes from a book about insects written by David Suzuki
Spiders are distant cousins of insects. Like insects, they. wear their skeletons on the
outside. But they have only two body parts. Their heads and thoraxes are joined together in
one part called a cephalothorax. They also have an abdomen. And here’s the difference that’s
easiest to spot between insects and spiders — all spiders have.eight legs. (As you already know,
insects get along fine with six.) Spiders belong to a class of animals called arachnida. Some of
the spiders’ relatives are ticks, mites and scorpions
Like insects, spiders lay eggs. But they don’t go through a larval stage. Little spiders
hatch out of the eggs looking just like their parents, except that they’re much smaller. As they
grow bigger, they shed their skins many times. If all the little spiders stayed in the place where
they hatched, they would have to fight each other for food. In fact, they might even eat each
other. They need to travel far away for food. How do you think they do it?
Spiders don’t have wings. But they do have a way to fly through the air when they need
to. They produce fine strong strands of silk from six spinnerets on their abdomens. The silk is
liquid, but it dries as soon as the air touches it. When the spiders want to travel, they raise their
abdomens and send out a strand of silk. The silk thread is caught by the breeze. The spider is
carried off through the air. This is called ballooning. Although most of them only go up a few
hundred metres, ballooning spiders have been found 4200 metres up in the air! Spiders also
use shorter silk strands as bridges from one place to another.
All spiders are hunters. They use their fangs to poison their prey. Then they suck out its
body juices, leaving a little dried husk. When we think of spiders, we think of webs in which
the spider sits waiting for a fly to be caught. But, while all spiders can make silk, not all
spiders spin webs to catch food.
Wolf spiders suddenly jump on their prey. The biggest spiders — the trapdoor spiders —
build burrows with hinged trapdoors, in the ground. The bola spider captures moths by hurling
a silk thread with a sticky glob on the end of it.

title: OC12 ENG — Questions 1-10
passage:
This passage is about plants.
Imagine you're standing in one spot and you can't move.
In fact, your feet are buried in the ground. The sun is beating down on your head. Pretty soon, you're
going to get very thirsty. But you can’t go anywhere to get yourself a drink.
This is just the way it is for most plants. While animals walk, run, hop, swim, slither and fly from
place to place, a plant stays in one spot all its life. It is held there by its root — a part of the plant that is
buried in the ground. Roots keep plants from being blown away in the wind. _ If you've ever tried to pull
up a dandelion, you know how well anchored in the earth a root can be.
A root is much more to the plant than’an anchor, though. The root gives the plant that drink it
needs. Water in the soil enters the root’and is carried up through the root, into the stem and out to the
plant's leaves and flowers. In the water are dissolved minerals that the plant needs to grow.
The root is so important to the plant that it is the first part to grow when a seed sprouts. The
. growing tip of the root is protected by a root cap. The moist root cap slips easily among the soil particles.
As roots branch out and spread through the ground, they make a web that holds the soil together.
There are two main kinds of roots. Fibrous roots are thin and have many branches. If you pull
up a fistful of grass you'll see fibrous roots. Tap roots are large thick roots with fine roots called root
hairs branching off them. Many tap roots act as food storage bins — and that food is good for us to eat too.
Carrots, parsnips and beets are tap roots. We pull them up before the plant has a chance to use the
stored food to make leaves, flowers and seeds.
How does the food get down to the roots to be stored? It travels through the stem. While water
and minerals are going up the stem to the leaves, sugary food made by the leaves is going down the stem
to all parts of the plant. lll this liquid flowing through the plant is called sap. Sap keeps the plant alive
the way blood flowing through your body keeps you alive.
You are held upright by a column of bones - your spine. A plant is held upright by its stem. The
stem is not kept stiff by bone, though, but by water. A plant that needs a drink will often droop and fall
over. After it is watered, it will soon stand straight again. Stems hold up the flowers and leaves where
they can get the air and sunlight they need.

The skating season had commenced unusually early: our boys were by no means
alone upon the ice. The afternoon was so fine that men, women and children, bent upon
enjoying the holiday, had flocked to the grand canal from far and near. St Nicholas had
evidently remembered the favourite pastime: shining new skates were everywhere to be
seen. Whole families were skimming their way to Haarlem, or Leyden, or the neighbouring
villages. The ice seemed fairly alive. Ben noticed the erect, easy carriage of the women, and
their picturesque variety of costume. There were the latest fashions, fresh from Paris,
floating past dingy, moth-eaten garments that had seen service through two generations;
coal-scuttle bonnets perched over freckled faces bright with holiday smiles; stiff muslin caps,
with wings at the sides flapping beside cheeks rosy with health and contentment; furs, too,
encircling the whites of throats; and scanty garments fluttering below faces ruddy with
exercise: in short, every quaint and comical mixture of dry-goods and flesh that Holland
could furnish seemed sent to enliven the scene.
There were belles from Leyden and fishwives from the border villages; cheese-women
from Gouda, and prim matrons from beautiful country seats on the Haarlemmer Meer.
Grey-headed skaters were constantly to be seen; wrinkled old women with baskets upon
their heads; and plump little toddlers on skates, clutching at their mother’s gowns. Some
women carried their babies upon their backs, firmly secured with a bright shawl. The effect
was pretty and graceful as they darted by, or sailed slowly past, now nodding to an
acquaintance, now chirruping and throwing soft baby-talk, to the muffled little ones they
carried.
Boys and girls were chasing each other, and hiding behind the one-horse sleds that,
loaded high with peat or timber pursued their cautious way along the track marked out as
“safe”. Beautiful, queenly women were there, enjoyment sparkling in their quiet eyes.
Sometimes a long file of young men, each grasping the coat of the before him, flew by with

slippers that were too large for him and down at heel; which was intelli gent of Mole, because

along in, both of you at once. Why, you must be perished. Well I never! Lost in the

title: OC25 ENG — Questions 21-25
passage:
My Lost Wedding Ring
I’d snorkelled hundreds of times in the lagoon and always loved seeing the beautiful fish and
marine life. This day I had been with my young son. I remember it was quite cold that week
and the waters were far cooler than ever before.
I remember having a few problems with my gear and that I had to readjust my face mask a
number of times. It was letting in water because my youngest son, who was only eight months
old, had been using it as a teether. I later realised it was this that led to the problem.
Anyway, we snorkelled for about an hour in the morning, going up around the point as we'd
earlier discovered these striped sea-horses that were simply ihttiguing. It didn’t take long for
our joy to change to anguish.
When I returned home I realised something was missing. My heart hiccuped as, while I was
removing my flippers, I noticed my wedding ring was gone. I know I had it when I left as I
hadn’t taken it off in the twenty years I’d been married. I couldn’t believe it. I was devastated!
I raced back to the lagoon, dragging along anyone who was available and we scoured the sandy
bottom for hours. Our fingers and toes became wrinkled prunes yet it was all in vain. The colder
water must have made my fingers smaller. The heavy gold ring must have fallen into the soft
sand or lay hidden among the coral and plants.
I never found my ring, despite repeated searches. I am still hopeful one day, perhaps after a
king tide, that it will be exposed and found. I bought another but I am still miserable. It will
never be the same as the one I really was married with.

Mr Bean-Everyone’s Favourite?
Garry Hastings: Thanks for talking to Text Chat Magazine. I hear you are an expert on Mr
Bean and how audiences respond to him.
Jill McGill: Well, I have spent a lot of time researching Rowan Atkinson’s
work.
Garry Hastings: So, does everyone love Mr Bean — or is it just everyone I know?
Jill McGill: Well, actually whilst Mr Bean is an amazingly popular character, not all
people find him funny. Instead, my research has found he seems to
appeal to a certain type of viewer.
Garry Hastings: Really? I think he’s hilarious and so do my kids.
Jill McGill: Yes, exactly. He is loved by children. They seem to find his simple
antics very amusing. Since he acts like a child much of the time they
can relate to him. Think of his teddy bear for instance and his inability
to carry out multi-staged tasks. Yet as they know he is an adult they
can understand it is silly.
Garry Hastings: So who doesn’t like Mr Bean?
Jill McGill: Well, it’s not so much they don’t like him it’s more that they do not
really respond. I’ve found very scientific, fac peo ple who like
clear rules and logic often find the humour fal Kewarn. They tend
to describe the antics as “stupid” and many even find the shows
frustrating. These people do not tend to enjoy physical humour, you
know like slap-stick, but favour more intellectual humour.
Garry Hastings: Wow? So does that make me a child then?
Jill McGill: No, no, no. There are many lucky people, like yourself, who are able to appreciate
all sorts of humour. You may well like a clever, intellectual Satire just as much,
Garry Hastings: Mmm I do. Well Jill, thanks for speaking with us today. I know our readers
love Rowan Atkinson’s Mr Bean.

title: OC27 ENG — Questions 6-10
passage:
Phar Lap
BEFORE Phar Lap’s second Melbourne Cup, gangsters were sending hitmen to stop him.
He was — and is — the only racehorse to become a national hero, firing the excitement of
Australia with his thundering race wins.
Phar Lap was named after the Thai word pharlap, meaning lightning, but he had a
nickname across the country — The Red Terror.
He seemed to be impossible to beat, and that was very dangerous.
Melbourne gangsters in the racing game were losing fortunes through Phar Lap and
becoming desperate.
Phar Laps’ trainer, Harry Telford, was warned of attacks through fire, acid and poison
darts as the Melbourne Cup of 1930 approached.
Strapper Tommy Woodcock was riding a pony and leading Phar Lap home from exercise
at Caulfield racecourse when he saw two suspicious men in an idling car.
Woodcock placed himself and the pony between the car and Phar Lap. The driver sped
past, blaring the horn as his mate fired a shotgun at the horse.
The shot splattered harmlessly over a high wooden fence, but Telford had had enough.
He took Phar Lap to the safety of Geelong until the race.
But the drama wasn’t over. Two hours before the race, Phar Laps float moved through
heavy rain out of Geelong, escorted by police motorcyclists.
And the engine died.
Telford and Woodcock took it in turns to crank the engine until it sputtered into life. They
reached Flemington racecourse no more than 30 minutes before the race was to start.
On that day four-year-old Phar Lap was carrying 9.12, a weight record for his age with
the odds of 11/8 on (meaning you put 11 units and if you win you only get 8 plus your
original 11). Phar Lap steamed through the race, winning effortlessly.
He was taken to America and he died in April 1932. There were unjustified rumours that
he had been poisoned by American gangsters.
Excerpt from ‘Legends Stories of Australia’ By Allan Baillie

Shane still remembers the day his dad lost his job. There was so much he didn’t understand.
So much he had to learn. And the learning was lonely, though lots of people tried to help.
Dad came home early that day. Shane was surprised but his mum didn’t seem to be. She
didn’t say, ‘What a nice surprise!’ or ‘Why are you home so early?’ She just stared, her dark
eyes somehow growing bigger and darker.
Dad said, ‘I’m redundant. They’ve made me redundant.’ And his voice was funny. Then
he said another word. He sounded frightened and sad and angry all at the same time. His
dad sounded frightened.
Redundant was the word that made his dad sound frightened. It made Shane think of the
big lumbering elephant at the circus. It sounded slow and clumsy. And somehow Dad
looked slow and clumsy, which he really wasn’t. He looked old and he looked awkward
when he put his arms around Mum.
Redundant. The elephant at the zoo always looked sad. Standing in the same spot,
marking time with its big solid feet, swaying slowly, staring at the bars and palm trees
painted on the concrete walls. Walking round the same track, past the same things, day after
day, year after year.
Redundant. Shane had seen an angry elephant in the wild tearing and trampling,
crushing everything in its path as it trumpeted its rage. It had scared him, even on TV.

A Special Island
Who doesn't enjoy a stay on a beautiful undeveloped island? Not many I suppose. When
that island is Rottnest Island off the Western Australian coast then there is little doubt. Almost
500,000 people visit this special island each year. The population of the island is about 150
but huge numbers of day trippers make the ninety minute journey from Perth or Fremantle on
ferries or charter boats that regularly carry eager tourists from Western Australia, the rest of
Australia and many countries.
It is an island where progress is measured in creating safe walking trails and ensuring that
the natural environment is protected well.
The total area of the island is about 2,000 hectares with pristine lakes taking up about 200
hectares. The crystal clear waters make for great swimming and boating activities. Snorkelling
with numerous fish and playful sea lions is a favourite activity. During the summer season
there can be as many as 5,000 people visiting at any one time.
The beauty of the island, the absence of high-rise buildings and noisy activities is, of
course, a major drawcard. Rottnest Island is home to a delightful creature - the quokka. It is
certain that this 30-40 centimetre high creature, somewhat like a furry rather overweight
wallaby, thrives well on Rottnest Island because of the absence of feral cats and wild dogs.
It is no wonder that many West Australians consider the island to be their favourite
holiday destination.

From The Raven by Edgar Allen Poe
Once upon a midnight dreary, while I pondered, weak and weary,
Over many a quaint and curious volume of forgotten lore,
While I nodded, nearly napping, suddenly there came a tapping,
As of someone gently rapping, rapping at my chamber door.
“ ‘Tis some visitor,” I muttered, “tapping at my chamber door;
Only this, and nothing more.”
Ah, distinctly I remember, it was in the bleak December,
And each separate dying ember wrought its ghost upon the floor.
Eagerly I wished the morrow; vainly I had sought to borrow
From my books surcease of sorrow, sorrow for the lost Lenore.
For the rare and radiant maiden whom the angels name Lenore,
Nameless here forevermore.
And the silken sad uncertain rustling of each purple curtain
Thrilled me--- filled me with fantastic terrors never felt before;
So that now, to still the beating of my heart, I stood repeating,
“ “Tis some visitor entreating entrance at my chamber door,
Some late visitor entreating entrance at my chamber door.
This it is, and nothing more.”
Presently my soul grew stronger; hesitating then no longer,
“Sir,” said I, “or madam, truly your forgiveness I implore;
But the fact is, I was napping, and so gently you came rapping,
And so faintly you came tapping, tapping at my chamber door,
That I scarce was sure I heard you. “Here I opened wide the door---
Darkness there, and nothing more.
Deep into the darkness peering, long I stood there, wondering, fearing
Doubting, dreaming dreams no mortals ever dared to dream before;
But the silence was unbroken, and the stillness gave no token,
And the only word there spoken was the whispered word,
Lenore?, This I whispered, and an echo murmured back the word,
“Lenore!” Merely this, and nothing more.
Back into the chamber turning, all my soul within me burning,
Soon again I heard a tapping, something louder than before,
“Surely,” said I, “surely, that is something at my window lattice.
Let me see, then, what thereat is, and this mystery explore.
Let my heart be still a moment, and this mystery explore.

Gracey didn’t sleep much that Saturday night before the final. I know ‘cause I could hear her
talking to Mum in their room along the hall. It was the middle of the night, getting later and
later. No use trying to work out what they were saying, of course, but Gracey was crying for
alittle while, and moving around, sometimes almost shouting, and other times so soft I wasn’t
sure she was speaking. And all the time, Mum’s voice was the same, a gentle murmur, like a
song, calming Gracey down.
I left my room and knocked on their door. Inside, Gracey was sitting on her bed with her
knees up to her chin and her arms wrapped tight round her legs. She always scrunched herself
into a ball like that when she was unhappy or frightened. I didn’t say anything, just sat on the
end of Gracey’s bed. It was sometimes like that when I came to listen to Mum and Gracey
talking. Gracey would look at me and witk, or smile or touch me for a second. It was like
she said, “Hello, Dougy. You can be here, part of us.” But that night Gracey was too upset,
too serious. She was saying, “But it’ll be so obvious if I don’t win. I'll stand out from the
others. Any of those white girls can come last and nobody will say anything, nobody will
even notice. Why do I have to be the one people will talk about?”
“TI know, it’s not fair,” said Mum in the same quiet voice I’d been hearing along the hall.
“That’s what blacks always have to put up with. Lots of noise when you win, lots of noise
when you lose. And they like to see you lose, too. Makes’em feel better. I seen it plenty of
times. They’re worried you might be better than them. That scares ’em inside. They really
don’t think much of you, and it’d be a terrible thing for you to beat ’em at something. That
just the way whities are. You got to worry "bout yourself.”
“It makes me angry,” said Gracey.
“Yes, it makes you angry. I know. But you got to make sure you’re angry at the white
blokes who treat you like that. No good being mad ’cause you’re a black. Just makes you

It was quiet in the pines except for the sound of the wind humming through their branches.
Robbie pushed his hands against a tree trunk and straightened one leg, then the other, behind
him. He could feel his calf muscles pulling and the bark digging into his palms. Next he
rested his heel on a stump and bent forward over his outstretched leg until the hamstring
muscle in his thigh warned him to go no further. He swapped legs and repeated the exercise.
His body had ceased revving like a car with the accelerator stuck. Robbie recognized the
calm he usually felt at this time before a race. His heart would pound again when he lined up
with the others at the start, but now he felt almost sleepy. He breathed deeply, shook his arms
and legs, and focused his mind on the course he, Mum and Tid had walked together this
morning.
It was a tight, twisting, hilly trail. A good cross-country course, the parents said. Robbie
remembered the narrow gateway a hundred metres from the start. He would have to be near
the lead if he didn’t want to wait his turn to get through there. Then there was a narrow track
with a barbed-wire fence on one side and a steep drop on the other. The course opened out
after that.
They had walked up a gradual slope, around a marker in a clump of trees and down a
gravel road, where the pebbles skidded under their feet, to a creek crossing. “Go for it up the
hill,” Mum had advised. “Careful coming down this gravel. Not too fast or you’ll go head

title: OC35 ENG — Questions 6-9
passage:
Lasseter’s Lost Reef
IN 1897, Harold Bell Lasseter was found unconscious in the desert southwest of Alice
Springs by an Afghan camel-driver — with some interesting rocks.
And the legend grew from there.
Lasseter said he had found a fabulously rich gold reef in the trackless desert out west, but
he would not say where. He wanted to lead an expedition to it.
For a while nobody seemed to be interested, but in 1911 there was an expedition — only
to be beaten back by the toughness of the country.
Lasseter tried one more time, in 1930, with a plane, a six-wheeled lorry and a team of
experts.
The plane crashed and Lasseter said they were over 250 kilometres off course.
The party on the ground battled on but finally decided to go home — except for Lasseter
and a dingo shooter, Paul Johns.
They pressed on, and Lasseter finally said he had found his reef. But he would not show
Johns where it was. They fought in the desert and Johns turned back, leaving Lasseter with
two camels.
The camels bolted from Lasseter, and though an Aboriginal tribe helped him he was
getting weaker and suffering from sandy-blight blindness.
He buried his papers under a tree marked ‘DIG’, crawled into a cave and died.
Nobody has ever found any trace of Lasseter’s reef.
From ‘Legends of Australia’ By Allan Baillie

The Silver Sword
This is an extract from a very exciting adventure story by lan Serraillier about refugee
children during the Second World War. It tells of their struggle to survive, avoid
capture, and of their seemingly hopeless search for their parents.
The current was swift. In the darkness the great wooded hills swept by. For a moment the
moon peeped from a cloud and turned the rippling surface of the stream to silver.
‘SERPRNE, moon’ Ruth muttered. ‘Don’t come out again until we’ve passed the village.’
Side by side the two canoes sped on.
On the left bank the line of hills curved downwards. Were those dim shapes houses? Had
they reached the village?
Again, the moon appeared. It had chosen quite the wrong moment, for this was indeed the
village, with houses crowded about both banks, and the left bank suddenly an open space
with lorries in it, they were so close together that they were almost touching, and there were
several rows of them. These must be the lorries that were to take the Polish refugees back
to Poland. With a tightening of fear in her throat, Ruth realised if they were spotted now, they
would be taken back, too.
‘Look out for the bridge’ said Edek.
He and Jan shot ahead, aiming for the centre of the three arches. Edging away from the
square, Ruth paddled towards the right-hand arch.
The water was noisy and Ruth did not hear the footsteps on the bridge. But she saw a man’s
shadow on the water and it was moving. She paddled frantically to get free.
‘The water’s coming in, | can feel it under me,’ said Bronia.
Aman shouted and his shadow leaned far out over the water.
The canoe was still across the base of the arch, with the water thrusting against each end,
threatening to break its back. She jabbed hard with the paddle and managed to ease it a
little.
The man was right overhead, shouting and waving, but she could not understand what he
was saying. In the distance a dog was barking.
A pair of legs dangled over the parapet and scraped against the stone. An American soldier.
With a last effort, she thrust at the stonework, and the canoe broke free. But the soldier had
clambered down and jumped into the water where it was shallow at the side. He caught the
paddle and clung on.
Ruth tugged, twisted, and then let go of it, the canoe swung sideways into the shadows
under the arch. The soldier, not expecting her to let go of it, toppled over backwards and fell
with a splash into the river.
As the canoe shot out beyond the bridge, Ruth realised that she was at the mercy of the
current. Bronia had no paddle and could not help.

passage:
This extract is taken from a book Minerals and Energy by Brian and Barbara Kennedy.
Gemstones, like other minerals, were mostly formed as a result of tremendous heat below the earth’s
surface. Some gemstones are more valuable than others.
Opals and sapphires are the only gemstones found in large quantities in Australia. Australia produces
almost all of the world’s opal. The main source is Coober Pedy in South Australia, but opals are also
found at Andamooka, South Australia, and at Lightning Ridge in New South Wales.
Opals are used mainly for jewellery and are very popular with overseas tourists, in spite of the fact
that some people believe that they bring bad luck.
Australia also produces half the world’s sapphires. The main fields are at Anakie in Queensland and
at Glen Innes and Inverell in New South Wales. Discoveries of high quality sapphires and an increase
in world demand have caused new interest in the sapphire mining industry in the Glen Innes-Inverell
area. Modern excavating machines are being used by large mining companies on their leases. Small
scale mining for sapphires has been in progress for most of the 20th century. Thailand is by far the
largest customer for Australian sapphires.
Chrysoprase, a green stone, is the most important gemstone after sapphires. It is found mainly in the
Marlborough district of Queensland.
Industrial diamonds exist in all states, especially in Western Australia and in New South Wales in the
Copeton-Bingara district. In the 1970s, the blue clay kimberlite pipes in which diamonds are formed
were discovered in the Kimberleys district of Western Australia. This led to the discovery of rich
diamond fields in the area. Because of their extreme hardness, diamonds can be used in high-speed
tools for cutting and drilling hard materials.
Gemstone fossicking is a very popular pastime for hundreds of Australians and there are many
valuable collections. Collectors are often lapidarists who cut, polish and set their own gemstones.

26 October 1768
Today we crossed the equator. King Neptune came aboard in the traditional fashion and
demanded tribute — a bottle of rum from all those unable to prove they have been south of the

13 November 1768
We have reached the Portuguese settlement at Rio de Janeiro. Although we have the royal
crown carved on our catheads, the governor, a stubborn fellow, refuses to believe that so humble
a vessel as Endeavour is a king’s ship on a scientific mission. He suspects us for a smuggler
and, much to the captain’s annoyance, has placed an armed guard. We are, he insists, to
purchase the ship’s provisions only through an appointed agent. This fellow has demanded the
highest prices.
25 November 1768
Captain Cook and the governor have exchanged a great many letters, but still the governor
will not bring himself to believe that we are sailing around the world merely to observe an
astronomical event.
The ship's company is not allowed ashore, but Mr Banks and Mr Parkinson, pretending to
be surgeon's mates seeking the purchase of medical supplies, have managed to botanise on
several occasions. They have brought on board over 300 plants. Many of them, Mr Banks says,

title: OC4 ENG — Questions 1-9
passage:
This is an article in a book called Why? What? Where?
Nobody knows what the first language was. But scientists feel quite sure that nobody speaks it today,
because all languages change and keep on changing as long as people use them. One language may
change in different ways in different places and grow into several separate languages.
People are always inventing new words. For example, radium was made-up as a name for a new
radioactive substance when scientists discovered it over a hundred years ago.
Words even change in one family. Children don’t always use words exactly the way their parents do.
They make small changes in the sounds or in the meaning. In time a lot of these little changes add up
and make big changes. If we could meet the people who spoke English five hundred years ago, we
probably couldn’t understand much of anything they said.
English was originally brought over by the Anglo-Saxons when they invaded Britain in the fifth and
sixth centuries. When Celtic monks came to convert the country, they brought some Latin and Greek
words with them; and in the ninth and tenth centuries Norse invaders from Scandinavia also brought
new words. The Norman invasion of 1066 introduced many new French words, which had originally
come from Latin.
The growth of learning, which began with the discoveries of the fifteenth and sixteenth century
explorers, led to many new words joining our language; and the development of science led to the
adoption of many Greek and Latin names for plants and animals and scientific inventions (e.g.
telephone). As knowledge grows, words are still being added.
Thus, English is a mixture of several languages. Scientists believe that these languages and many
others all grew out of the same ancestor language which they call Indo-European. Nobody speaks
Indo-European now, but some of its descendants, besides English, are German, Latin, French, Greek,
Russian and many of the different tongues spoken in India.

title: OC2023|OC13 ENG — Questions 1-9
passage:
This is an Aboriginal legend.
Very early in the beginning of the Dreamtime there were no kangaroos in this land.
A group of men were out hunting one day, when suddenly they were hit by the
worst windstorm they had ever experienced. Large trees were blown over, small ones
were carried away into the sky, and huge boulders were tossed around like pebbles in
a children’s game.
The hunters were lucky to reach the safety of a cave. They sat in its shelter and
watched the storm take its course. After a while they were amazed to see a band of
animals being carried across the sky by the wind. They had never seen animals of this
sort before.
The men shook their heads in bewilderment as they discussed this extraordinary
sight, and realised that the creatures must have been brought by the wind from a distant
place that no-one in their group had ever visited.
The animals were quite large and covered in fur. They had small heads and short
front legs. It was obvious that they were very distressed at being blown through the wild
air. Frantically they kept stretching out their hind legs and their tails in an effort to make
contact with the ground.
The hunters watched keenly from their cave as the animals strained and battled
desperately against the wind. At last some of them did manage to find a toehold and
tailhoid and anchor themselves to solid earth. The windstorm began to pass, and the
animals, which had forced their way down were left behind.
The watching hunters could now see that the animals had overstretched
themselves in their desperation to reach the ground. Their hind legs and tails were
elongated out of all proportion to the rest of their bodies. It really looked quite strange,
but the animals themselves did not seem particularly upset. Perhaps they were so
pleased to be on steady ground that nothing else mattered.
So far the hunters had been watching all this as an amazing event that would
make a good story. They took it for granted that the animals would run away
immediately, trying to get back to their own land.
It seemed that although the animals were tired and bewildered they were also
inquisitive. They began to look for shade, grass and water, and quickly found them
This was exactly the sort of place they liked and it soon became clear that they had
decided to stay.
-—— Reading page 1

title: OC2023|OC12 ENG — Questions 1-6
passage:
This passage is about plants.
Imagine you’re standing in one spot and you can’t move.
In fact, your feet are buried in the ground. The sun is beating down on your head.
Pretty soon, you’re going to get very thirsty. But you can’t go anywhere to get yourself
a drink.
This is just the way it is for most plants. While animals walk, run, hop, swim,
slither and fly from place to place, a plant stays in one spot all its life. It is held there
by its root — a part of the plant that is buried in the ground. Roots keep plants from
being blown away in the wind. If you've ever tried to pull up a dandelion, you know
how well anchored in the earth a root can be.
A root is much more to the plant than an anchor, though. The root gives the
plant that drink it needs. Water in the soil enters the root and is carried up through
the root, into the stem and out to the plant’s leaves and flowers. In the water are
dissolved minerals that the plant needs to grow.
The root is so important to the plant that it is the first part to grow when a seed
sprouts. The growing tip of the root is protected by a root cap. The moist root cap
slips easily among the soil particles. As roots branch out and spread through the
ground, they make a web that holds the soil together.
There are two main kinds of roots. Fibrous roots are thin and have many
branches. If you pull up a fistful of grass you'll see fibrous roots. Tap roots are large
thick roots with fine roots called root hairs branching off them. Many tap roots act as
food storage bins — and that food is good for us to eat too. Carrots, parsnips and
beets are tap roots. We pull them up before the plant has a chance to use the stored
food to make leaves, flowers and seeds.
How does the food get down to the roots to be stored? It travels through the
stem. While water and minerals are going up the stem to the leaves, sugary food
made by the leaves is going down the stem to all parts of the plant. All this liquid
flowing through the plant is called sap. Sap keeps the plant alive the way blood
flowing through your body keeps you alive.
You are held upright by a column of bones — your spine. A plant is held upright
by its stem. The stem is not kept stiff by bone, though, but by water. A plant that
needs a drink will often droop and fall over. After it is watered, it will soon stand
straight again. Stems hold up the flowers and leaves where they can get the air and
sunlight they need.
-—— Reading page 1

This passage is from “Charlotte’s Web” by E.B. White, a story about a girl who lives ona
farm in America.
The early summer days on a farm are the happiest and fairest days of the year. Lilacs bloom
and make the air sweet, and then fade. Apple blossoms come with the lilacs and the bees visit
round among the apple trees. The days grow warm and soft. School ends, and children have
time to play and to fish for trout in the brook. Avery often brought a trout home in his pocket,
warm and stiff and ready to be fried for supper.
Now that school was over, Fern visited the barn almost every day, to sit quietly on her stool. The
animals treated her as an equal. The sheep lay calmly at her feet.
Around the first of July, the work horses were hitched to the mowing machine, and Mr Zuckerman
climbed into the seat and drove into the field. All morning you could hear the rattle of the
machine as it went round and round, while the tall grass fell down behind the cutter bay in long
green swathes.
Next day if there was no thunder shower, all hands would help rake and pitch and load, and the
hay would be carried to the barn in the high hay wagon, with Fern and Avery riding at the top of
the load. Then the hay would be hoisted, sweet and warm, into the big loft, until the whole barn
seemed like a wonderful bed of fimothy and clover. It was fine to jump in, and perfect to hide
in. And sometimes Avery would find a little grass snake in the hay and would add it to the other
things in his pocket.
Early summer days are a jubilee time for birds. In the fields, around the house, in the barn, in
the woods, in the swamp — everywhere love and songs and nests and eggs. From the edge of
the woods, the white throated sparrow, (which must come all the way from Boston) calls,” Oh,
Peabody, Peabody, Peabody!” On an apple bough, the phoebe teeters and wags its tail and says,
“Phoebe, phoe-bee!” The song sparrow, who knows how brief and lovely life is, says, “Sweet,
sweet, sweet interlude; sweet, sweet, sweet interlude.” If you enter the barn, the swallows swoop
down from their nests and scold. “Cheeky, cheeky!” they say.
In early summer there are plenty of things for a child to eat and drink and suck and chew.
Dandelion stems are full of milk, clover heads are loaded with nectar, the Frigidaire is full of ice-
cold drinks. Everywhere you look is life; even the little ball of spit on the weed stalk, if you poke
it apart, has a green worm inside it. And on the underside of the leaf of the potato vine are the
bright orange eggs of the potato bug.

WESTERN SWAMP TURTLE
This turtle, also called the western swamp tortoise, is found only in two swamps in Perth,
Western Australia and is possibly Australia’s most endangered reptile. There are less than
fifty of these animals still living in the wild.
The western swamp turtle is about 15 centimetres long, and has a short neck and a broad,
flat head, which is covered with a rough helmet. It has a square shell, which is brown on top
and olive-brown or yellow underneath.
In November or December, the female lays three to five hard-shelled eggs in a nest dug a
few centimetres below the surface of the ground. The hatchlings emerge between May and
June and may live for more than fifty years.
During the wet winter months, this turtle lives in the swamps. During summer they take
refuge from the sun, spending the hot months in holes in the ground, or under deep leaf litter.
The western swamp turtle feeds on small tadpoles and insect larvae found in and around
the swamp.
To try and ensure that the western swamp turtle does not become extinct, a captive breeding
program has been established at Perth Zoo, and a number of young turtles were born there
in 1989. This breeding program may be the only way that the western swamp turtle will
survive.
The turtle’s natural habitat lies right on the border of the city of Perth and its home has been
destroyed to make way for houses, office blocks and for agriculture. Clay mining has also
destroyed the home of the western swamp turtle.

title: OC2023|OC3 ENG — Questions 10-19
passage:
This is an obituary from the Sydney Morning Herald 10" January 2008.
P.K. Sethi 1927-2008
Millions of amputees in developing countries owe thanks to Dr P.K. Sethi for his invention
of an affordable prosthetic foot, which has enabled them to lead normal lives.
The Jaipur foot, which has never been patented, is available in more than 25 countries,
mostly poor and many with large numbers of landmine victims. Unlike many high-priced
prostheses in developed countries it can be made by traditional craftsmen, last more than five
years and costs about $34.
Pramod Karan Sethi, who has died in Jaipur, India at 80, was born in the ancient northern
Indian city of Benares, on the banks of the Ganges. His father was a professor of physics at
Benares Hindu University. On completing his medical education in India and Britain, Sethi
became a lecturer in surgery at a Medical College in Jaipur.
He became an orthopaedic surgeon by default. In 1958, his institution was about to be
inspected for accreditation, and since there was no department of orthopaedics, he was asked
to start one at once. He always maintained that not being a qualified orthopaedic surgeon helped
him produce something that was genuinely new.
Sethi came up with his invention after years of research. He was helped by
Ramachandra Sharma, a semiliterate craftsman.
They made a foot of vulcanised rubber but found it too heavy and stiff. So, they filled
the shell with sponge rubber and modified the design.
Since 1971 when Sethi presented the design to British orthopaedic surgeons at Oxford,
the Jaipur foot has revolutionised lives in war-torn countries. It is very flexible, allowing the
wearer to run, climb trees and pedal a bicycle.
The Jaipur foot was first used outside India in Afghanistan, which had the highest number
of amputees in the world after Russian landmines caused thousands of wounds.
Sethi is survived by his wife, Sulochana, a son and three daughters.

Our transport revolution
WHILE views might differ about what should be built first, the massive Victorian
Transport Plan to be announced today is crucial to ensuring our city’s future.
Following almost a decade of promises, and many earlier “plans” to fix greater
Melbourne’s transport woes, this blueprint could finally be a way forward.
It includes a $6 billion link — with tunnels — between the Eastern Freeway at Bulleen and
the Western Ring Road at Greensborough.
Rail would be extended from Epping to South Morang. Footscray and Caulfield would
be linked by underground tracks, and $650 million would be spent on new trains.
Money is allocated to work out how Hoddle St traffic might move faster, and $100 million
over 12 years has been set aside for bicycle paths.
Part of Sir Rod Eddington’s proposed east-west road link is in the mix.
Melbournians are expected to make almost three million extra car trips daily in the next
25 years. More than 900,000 extra trips will be taken on public transport over the same
period.
Transport is a city’s veins and arteries. Without it, we could not work or visit friends or
enjoy ourselves.
And as Melbourne becomes more popular and sprawls ever farther, excellent systems
will be increasingly important.
Aspects of them will always be controversial, but we have no alternative but to build and
pay for them.
Assaults down
THAT CBD assaults on Friday and Saturday nights in October and November dropped
by 24 per cent compared with last year is encouraging.
The Safe Streets Taskforce program begun last month appears to be working, even if
the numbers of drunks remains disturbing.
Police have issued more than 1440 penalty notices for offensive behaviour and urinating
in public. And, despite extra officers on the streets and CCTV vans, Herald Sun reporters
have witnessed this weekend shocking alcohol-fuelled scenes.
Residents of outer suburbs rarely see such things. They are the happiest Melburnians,
according to Leader Newspapers’ annual My Melbourne survey.
If only young people who play — play up — in the CBD could adopt some of the communal
responsibility shown in such places as Eltham and Warrandyte.
Herald Sun (Melbourne, Australia) 12-08-2008

This article comes from a book about insects written by David Suzuki
Spiders are distant cousins of insects. Like insects, they wear their skeletons on the
outside. But they have only two body parts. Their heads and thoraxes are joined together
in one part called a cephalothorax. They also have an abdomen. And here’s the
difference that’s easiest to spot between insects and spiders — all spiders have eight legs.
(As you already know, insects get along fine with six.) Spiders belong to a class of
animals called arachnida. Some of the spiders’ relatives are ticks, mites and scorpions
Like insects, spiders lay eggs. But they don’t go through a larval stage. Little
spiders hatch out of the eggs looking just like their parents, except that they’re much
smaller. As they grow bigger, they shed their skins many times. If all the little spiders
stayed in the place where they hatched, they would have to fight each other for food. In
fact, they might even eat each other. They need to travel far away for food. How do you
think they do it?
Spiders don’t have wings. But they do have a way to fly through the air when they
need to. They produce fine strong strands of silk from six spinnerets on their abdomens.
The silk is liquid, but it dries as soon as the air touches it. When the spiders want to
travel, they raise their abdomens and send out a strand of silk. The silk thread is caught
by the breeze. The spider is carried off through the air. This is called ballooning.
Although most of them only go up a few hundred metres, ballooning spiders have been
found 4200 metres up in the air! Spiders also use shorter silk strands as bridges from
one place to another.
All spiders are hunters. They use their fangs to poison their prey. Then they suck
out its body juices, leaving a little dried husk. When we think of spiders, we think of
webs in which the spider sits waiting for a fly to be caught. But, while all spiders can
make silk, not all spiders spin webs to catch food.
Wolf spiders suddenly jump on their prey. The biggest spiders — the trapdoor
spiders — build burrows with hinged trapdoors, in the ground. The bola spider captures
moths by hurling a silk thread with a sticky glob on the end of it. -

girlfriend, Bob puts his hand up to look after her three kids when she suddenly

Inane, unfunny and totally tired, The Spy Next Door is the worst new release of

I use a fan-forced oven. Val
A Because Christmas cakes are usually dense with fruit,
they take a long time to cook, therefore the top of the cake
is exposed to more direct heat than the rest of the cake.
To prevent this, sprinkle or finely mist water over the top
of the cake before putting it in the oven. After the first
30 minutes baking, cover the top of the cake with foil or
brown paper and place a container of water in the oven to
create a little steam during the cooking. Make sure you
refill it during the cooking process. Fan-forced ovens tend
to dry rich fruit cakes more than conventional cooking.
Cook at a moderately slow temperature and let the cake
cool in the tin for 30 minutes or more before turning out.
As the cake cools, any cracks usually close over.

Recruits, returnees and rookies go on show
By GREG BAUM
THE ball fell to Ben Cousins in the middle of the incongruously lush oval at Gosch’s Paddock.
He gathered, arched his back in that familiar way and ran in a wide semi-circle. Now in space,
he paused momentarily, then accelerated again, on a new course, straight towards goal.
Ahead, other players hastily rearranged themselves. “Watch the dish,” urged a man in the
crowd of around 1500, standing three-deep around the fence.
Cousins’ “‘dish” (that is, pass) began wide, but curved as if on an unseen wind, unerringly
onto the chest of the helmeted Graham Polak, leading hard into the forward pocket.
It would be gilding the lily to say that the crowd roared, but it certainly clapped
appreciatively.
Cousins and Polak played together for Richmond yesterday. It was an irresistible turn of
events since one was a drug addict out in the football cold three months ago and the other
was — and still is — rehabilitating from head injuries after being wrong-footed by a tram last
June.
But it was qualified by all these certainties: it was February 5, too early even for March
championship; it was 27 degrees, too sultry for football; the Nylex clock that formed part of
the backdrop said so.
Cousins played half a game, then was whisked away by car, his now customary blaze of
secrecy. Polak played about 40 minutes. Matthew Richardson was long gone, back, bare-
chested, across the scorched parkland to the Tiger’s Punt Road HQ; one, dominant quarter
was enough to clear his few cobwebs.

and transport systems were integrated. This progress came at a personal Cost to King.

the Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to Martin Luther King for his efforts to achieve justice
for the black people of America. Yet, at the time, King was experiencing great difficulties.
His efforts were scorned by the more militant black organisations and at the same time,
his work was being resistance to the war in Vietnam. On 4th April, 1968, Martin Luther
King was assassinated. Although his life was cut short, his achievements were formidable.

How have games changed?
Graphics are the most obvious evolution for games, but multi-player has completely
revolutionised the industry when you compare it to the ‘80s and early ‘90s. While many
detractors still believe games are anti-social, the reality today is that they are incredibly social.

tiresome, there ain’t no peace like the greatest peace - the peace of the Lord’s hand holding you.

It was a particularly humid late afternoon in sixth grade and I had been left for dead at school. Teachers,
maintenance staff, even the sanitary-disposal van had left the grounds, leaving me in the company of
a peer that I had spoken to only once throughout the entire year (and that was only to ask if she could
please stop using my treasured connector pens). She was prematurely developed, buxom girl who
spoke in a deep, husky voice and had sun-bleached hair from over-tanning.
Let’s just say she was the antithesis of me.
She repeated her revelation, this time with more gusto.
“You shave them! That’s so gross... I can’t believe you’d do that!”
“T don’t shave them!”
I tried to explain to her that I was just born that way and that most Chinese girls don’t have much hair
on their arms, save for a fine fuzz. However, she had already lost herself in a state of cackling delirium
— clearly overwhelmed by her own hilarity and the freakish nature of my body.
I crossed my arms in defiance, but after realising this would probably expose their hairlessness more,
made to hide them under my Lion King swimming bag, which contained chlorine soaked hand-me-
down togs that literally hung off me if I didn’t knot them up at the back. It had not been a good sports
lesson; once again I was isolated in the sixth lane with a pair of flippers and a kick-board, while my
friends mastered tumble-turns and learnt to open their eyes underwater. I watched them through my
blurry, steamed-up, over-sized goggles, and saw their hair floating around them with an ethereal
quality that mine, tightly contained in a cap full of baby powder, simply could not achieve. I had
pleaded for hours with my mum about the cap, but she had remained adamant:
“When you put the powder in, it makes the can come off so much easier! Like magic!” she explained.
“But it looks like dandruff... or nits.”
“Ai-ya! You know what the herbalists say. You'll get a headache with wet hair. Do you want to get
sick from having a wet head all day?”
“Tt it’s normal, yeah!”

passage:
The Sanctuary
Colin Thiele, 1992
When Storm Boy went walking along the beach, or over the sandhills, or in the sanctuary, the
birds were not afraid. They knew he was a friend. The pelicans sat in a row, like a lot of important
old men with their heavy paunches sagging, and rattled their beaks drily in greeting; the moor-
hens fussed and chattered; the ibises Gul the air into Strips as they jerked their curved beaks up
and down; and the blue crane stood in silent dignity like a tall thin statue as Storm Boy went past.
But one morning Storm Boy found everything in iproaPand contusion. Three or four men had
gone into the sanctuary. They had found some pelican nests- wide, rough nests of sticks, grass,
and pelican feathers as big as turkey quills — and they had killed two of the big birds nesting
there. After that they had scattered everything wildly with their boots, kicking and shouting and
picking up the white eggs and throwing them about until they were all broken. Then they had
gone off laughing.
Storm Boy crept forward in fear and anger. From behind a tussock he looked round sadly at the
ruin and destruction. Then, just as he was about to run back to tell Fingerbone to fill his
blunderbuss with salt, he heard a faint rustling and crying, and there under the broken nests were
three tiny pelicans — still alive. Storm Boy picked them up and carefully hurried back with them.

H.M.S. BELLEROPHON
On June 1 1815 an attempt was made by the French to break the blockade of Europe
imposed by the British navy. France under Napoleon had already conquered most of
Europe but was short of food. A convoy of American grain ships escorted by fleet of French
warships attempted to penetrate the blockade and unload at the, French port of Brest. The
convoy was intercepted however by the British fleet commanded by Admiral Howe. Agreat
engagement ensued and for many hours the battles raged. Although some of the grain
ships managed f@llimp into harbour, eventually the ue sr ce inflicting
heavy losses on the French. | | | :
One of the British warships participating in the battle was Bellerophon. With 74 guns,
Bellerophon, the flagship of the Fleet, was possibly the finest warship afloat at the time.
The ship was in the thick of the battle for some hours, taking a bad battering, and her
causalities included the captain, Rear Admiral Parsley, who lost a leg to a cannon shot. On
board Bellerophon at the time was a young officer, scarcely more than a boy, acting as
Aide-de-camp to the Admiral. His name was Mathew Flinders.
In between bouts of destruction caused by French broadsides and the noise and chaos
of the Bellerophon’s own guns being fired as the battle raged back and forth, Flinders was
able to find time to jot down notes on the course of the battle for the Admiral. This was one
of his official duties. The description in his journal, copied up at the end of the battle, runs
to 40 pages and is regarded by naval historians as the best account of this most famous
battle. From it they are able to judge exactly the course of the engagement.
Flinders survived the ‘Battle of the Glorious First’ and, at a later date of course, became
quite famous in a different way as a navigator and explorer although still serving as an
officer in the Royal Navy. The Bellerophon too \ived on to carry out at least one more
famous voyage when she carried Napoleon from France to Portsmouth before he was
transported as a prisoner to the Island of St Helena in the Atlantic Ocean.

ANCIENT MURDER MYSTERY SOLVED?
TUTANKHAMEN was only ten years old when he became the Pharaoh of Egypt around
3300 years ago. The cause of his death, at a young age, has been an enduring mystery that
has puzzled historians, archaeologists, forensic scientists and even police detectives ever
since his mummified body was uncovered in 1922.
The discovery of Tutankhamen’s tomb fllelléd "speculation about the possible cause of his
death. Unlike most other Egyptian tombs, although the antechamber and annex had been
disturbed, Tutankhamen’s burial chamber had been untouched by tomb raiders or vandals.
it was filled with fabulous treasures, including a priceless gold funeral mask. However the
tomb was small and clearly unfinished in parts, which gave rise to the theory that the young
pharaoh had died suddenly and the tomb had been hastily prepared. This led experts to
surmise that Tutankhamen had been murdered.
Tutankhamen’s mummy was first examined by Dr Douglas Derry. Derry established that the
king had been about eighteen when he died. In 1963 Tutankhamen’s body was x-rayed by
R.G.Harrison, an anatomist and an authority on mummies. The x-ray revealed a possible
skull fracture suggesting that Tutankhamen may have been killed by a blow to the back of
the head. This finding was strongly supported by further tests in the mid-1990s which led to
a hunt for a long-dead murderer.
Bob Brier, a researcher from Long Island University and two former US police officers, Greg
Cooper and Mike King, were just some of the people who became obsessed with identifying
King Tutankhamen’s killer. Using modern forensic and profiling techniques they began their
own investigation. There were several suspects: Ay, Tutankhamen’s chief adviser who
succeeded him as Pharaoh; Maya, his treasurer; Horemheb, his general who also became
Pharaoh after Ay’s death; and Ankhesenamen, Tutankhamen’s wife, who later named Ay.
The investigator agreed that Ay had the most to gain from Tutankhamen’s death and felt
satisfied that they had correctly identified the ancient assassin. However, many
Egyptologists remained sceptical and subsequent tests have suggested a completely new
scenario: King Tutankhamen may have died from an infection in a badly broken leg.
A research team, led by Zahi Hawass, the Chairman of Egypt’s Supreme Council of
Antiquities, examined images of the mummy taken from a CT scan and concluded that there
was no evidence of a blow to the back of the head, and therefore no indication of foul play.
The most recent theory that Tutankhamen died as a result of a broken leg may help to solve
another, smaller mystery: why, among the glorious treasures in Tutankhamen’s tomb, there
were also 130 walking sticks!

Wealth data tells a tale of two cities
Tim Colebatch
TWO towers symbolise the gap between affluence and deprivation in Melbourne. Barely three
kilometres apart, fringing the city in opposite directions, the 2006 Census shows them as polar
opposites of socio-economic advantage and disadvantage in our state.
The desirable tower is Yarra's Edge, the award-winning "urban village" developed by Mirvac ‘on
the old site of South Wharf, in Docklands. On a wide-ranging index of measures, the Bureau of
Statistics ranks it the most socioeconomically advantaged community in Victoria.
The tough tower is an old Housing Commission block of flats, on the corner of Melrose and
Canning Streets in North Melbourne, down from Racecourse Road. Many of its residents are
refugees, Islam is the main religion, and only 39 people have a job.
From census data collected in more than 9000 districts throughout Victoria, the Bureau has
constructed an index of socioeconomic advantage and disadvantage, ranking each district —
ranging in size from city blocks to large areas of farmland and forest — from 1 to 9055.
The index covers 21 variables, such as the proportion of households with high or low incomes,
the proportion with broadband or no internet access, how many people work as professionals
or labourers, the size of mortgages and rent payments, the number of bedrooms, and
occupants’ qualifications.
At both ends, the extremes are clustered in towers edging the city. Six of the 10 most
advantaged districts are new apartment blocks in Docklands, Southbank, Port Melbourne and
the CBD. And nine of the 10 most disadvantaged are old Housing Commission towers in North
Melbourne, Ascot Vale, Kensington and Collingwood.
One difference leaps out: at the Melrose Street flats, only 25% of people were born in Australia,
as against 65% at Yarra's Edge. And, at Yarra's Edge, the migrants come mostly from the US,
Malaysia and England; at Melrose Street, from Vietnam, China, Somalia and Eritrea.
While tax data last week showed the taxman still makes his biggest hauls in Portsea, Toorak,
and Brighton, the Bureau's index, finds the new towers along the Yarra and the waterfront have
Melbourne's greatest concentration of well-off people.
The second best collection of Melburnians lives in Southbank just behind the National Gallery.
Southbank and Docklands each have two collectors' districts in the top 10, which also include
Beacon Cove in Port Melbourne (sixth) and the city block bounded by La Trobe, Queen,
Lonsdale and William streets.
Reading Skills page 5
Of the traditional homes of wealthy Melburnians, the river end of St Georges Road, Toorak,
remains pre-eminent. The Bureau ranks it the third, closely followed by another riverside area
along Alexandra Avenue, South Yarra. The Monomeath Avenue area of Canterbury was also
in the top 10, as was the part of Kew heading to the river along Molesworth Street.
The top 10 areas by postcode were Docklands, the World Trade Centre, Canterbury, East
Melbourne, Southbank, Brighton, Toorak, Malvern, Queens Road and Portsea.
The poorest postcodes were mostly in the bush: Korong Vale and Nyah West in the north-west,
Cressy in the Western District, and Nowa Nowa and Longwarry in Gippsland. Melbourne's most
disadvantaged suburbs are Braybrook, Frankston and Broadmeadows.
The Age, March 27 2008

Director: Patrick Tatopoulos (feature debut)
Starring: Bill Nighy, Michael Sheen, Phona Mitra, Kevin Grevioux
>Gone to howl and never coming back
OH, THE vagaries of franchise filmmaking. When the going is good, the talent will happily
front up for a sequel. When the talent goes elsewhere, the only option is to persuade
whoever is left to do a prequel. Such is the sorry fate which has befallen the Underworld
series. You remember the first two flicks, right? You don’t? OK, here’s what you missed.
Kate Beckinsale in a rubber catsuit. Scott Speedman and a posse of greasy-haired dudes
with coloured contact lenses. An ancient blood feud between fashion-victim vampires and
not-so-stylish werewolves.
Whew. Classic stuff, huh? Well, it used to fill the time between visits from Wesley Snipes
and the Blade gang. However, now that Beckinsale and Speedman have better things to do
with their time, former support players Bill Nighy and Michael Sheen have been bumped up
the billing. For their trouble, these stalwart British thesps have been saddled with a cheap
and cheerless cash-in that should bury the whole underworld thing once and for all. In Rise
of the Lycans, the narrative clock is wound back a century or five to explain how vampires
and werewolves came to hate each other so. Unremarkably, what follows sucks and bites
in equal measure. Big-boss vamp Viktor (Nighy) gets his black velvet cape in a twist when
he discovers his headstrong daughter Sonia (Rhona Mitra, prepared to show a little more
and emote a lot less than her predecessor Beckinsale) has been canoodling with the hairy
he-man hellhound Lucian (Sheen). After building up this Transylvanian standoff with a pile
of claptrap about keeping all spooky species strictly separated, the film then devolves into a
wonky Braveheart for werewolves.
Sadly, Sheen is no Mel Gibson. Now, Sheen is a fine actor. On the strength of his work as
David Frost in Frost/Nixon and Tony Blair in The Queen, you could easily argue he is one of
the best in the business at the moment. However, no amount of growling, howling or baby
oil on his biceps can establish Sheen’s credentials as a rough ’n’ tumble man of action.
Nothing else of note to mention here, save for a hulking man-mountain named Kevin
Grevioux, whose voice is so unbelievably deep he could short-circuit a
subwoofer merely by clearing his throat.
