passage:
On the Darling River
The Darling - which is either a muddy gutter or a second Mississippi - is about six
times as long as the distance, in a straight line, from its head to its mouth. The state of the
river is vaguely, but generally understood to depend on some distant and foreign phenomena,
to which bushmen refer in an offhand tone of voice as "the Queenslan' rains", which seem to
be held responsible, in a general way, for most of the outback trouble.
It takes less than a year to go upstream by boat to Walgett or Bourke in a dry season
because the river is then a string of waterholes. After a while the passengers get sick of
climbing out of the boat while it is carried to the next long waterhole. They get sick of being
stuck in the same sort of place, in the same old way; they grow weary of seeing the same old
timer drop his swag on the bank opposite whenever the boat ties up for wood; they get tired
of lending him tobacco, and listening to his ideas, which are limited in number and narrow
in conception.
It shortens the journey to get out and walk; but then you will have to wait so long for
your luggage - unless you hump it with you.
We heard of a man who determined to stick to a Darling boat and travel the whole
length of the river. He was a newspaper man. He started on his voyage of discovery one
Easter in flood-time, and a month later the captain got bushed between the Darling and the
South Australian border. The water went away before he could find the river again, and he
left his boat in a scrub. They had a cargo of rations, and the crew stuck to the craft while the
tucker lasted; when it gave out they rolled up their swags and went to look for a station, but
didn't find one. The captain would study his watch and the sun, rig up dials and make out
courses, and follow them without success. They ran short of water, and didn't smell any for
weeks; they suffered terrible privations, and lost three of their number, not including the
newspaper man. There were even dark hints of considering the drawing of lots in connection
with something too terrible to mention. They crossed a thirty-mile plain at last, and sighted a
young Aboriginal girl. She led them to a boundary-rider's hut where they were taken in and
provided with rations.
Later on a syndicate was formed to explore the country and recover the boat; but
they found her thirty miles from the river and about eighteen from the nearest waterhole deep
enough to float her so they left her there.

title: STT2023|STT51 ENG — Questions 11-16
passage:
Environmental Dangers
Two introduced animals have created a danger to our environment and continue to
do so despite government efforts to overcome the problems they are causing.
The buffalo was introduced from Indonesia between 1825 and 1843. It bred
successfully in regions of the Northern Territory which perfectly suited its needs. The wetland
areas of the Northern Territory are at risk from these animals. They have caused
considerable damage and it is estimated that over 6,000 hectares of paper bark forests have
been utterly destroyed. When these animals move from place to place they create deep
channels in the water-logged areas. The banks of the water courses are damaged. This
means that the natural banks can no longer function effectively. In the dry season water from
the ocean breaks into these areas. The plant and animal life that cannot tolerate the increase
in salinity can no longer survive or are greatly reduced. Although steps are being taken to
minimise the damage, there are still an estimated 80,000 of these animals. The damage
they continue to cause to swamps, fresh water springs and nesting sites of water birds is
considerable.
Introduced with the arrival of the First Fleet, the feral goat causes problems over a
much wider area than the buffalo. Early settlers used them for meat and milk. Today it is
estimated that there are 7 million feral goats in Australia. They are found in approximately
half the area of Australia. Control of feral goats is almost impossible as they can exist on
virtually all types of vegetation. Properties and National Parks are at risk as mobs of feral
goats ravage the natural vegetation to such an extent that areas are reduced to a barren
landscape. Water supplies for stock and native animals are often reduced to muddy bogs,
and, in the extreme heat can be completely dry. Their habit of stripping trees and grasses
causes severe erosion of vast tracts of land, wind erosion in the dry months and erosion by
water when flooding rains occur.
Both these pests require a prolonged and expensive eradication program to avoid
the environmental damage which will continue.

Australia
The Age Newspaper
Jim Schembri, reviewer, December 2, 2008
There are moments while watching Baz Luhrmann’s over-sized, over-long Outback weepie
Australia when one wonders if there are any tablecloth clichés about Australia that have been
missed.
No, it all seems to be there. The horses. The cattle. The dust. The rugged Aussie loner. The
Aborigine standing on one leg in a loincloth. The beer. The roos. About the only thing missing
is a bloke named Bruce.
It may not be the stuff from which classic films are typically born but such clichés provide a
great featherbed of easy-to-digest references for the type of sweeping melodramatic saga
designed to appeal to the lucrative “chick flick” market and to foreign audiences eager for an
attractive holiday destination.
By these measures Australia cannot be seriously faulted. With its open links to the tourism
industry, the film is a great ad. As entertainment, the saga, cringe-inducing as it often is,
eventually delivers the type of big, crowd-pleasing, teary emotional pay-off that makes its
many longueurs and overcooked characters worth enduring, even if the film is 30 minutes
too long.
Set in the Northern Territory in 1939 on a remote cattle station with the fairytale name of
Faraway Downs, Australia tells of the forging of a family. Lady Sarah Ashley (Nicole Kidman)
is the prissy English aristocrat who arrives to make a go of the station after the murder of her
husband, allegedly by a blackfella called King George (David Gulpilil). Helping her take her
cattle to Darwin is the enigmatic Drover (Hugh Jackman), a no-nonsense piece of calendar-
worthy, girl-baiting Aussie beefcake.
Glueing the story together is Nullah (Brandon Walters), a sweet-faced little boy of mixed
blood whose stateless status and dubious parentage serves as the lightning rod for the film’s
overarching themes of racism, responsibility, love and reconciliation.

title: STT2023|STT52 ENG — Questions 12-16
passage:
Early Forms of Parliament
The evolution of the parliamentary system used in Australia can be traced back to
the United Kingdom. Long before the term United Kingdom was used, the Anglo-Saxons and
Jutes from mainland Europe were settling in England. They brought with them a type of self-
government that suited the needs of the scattered tribes. There was a meeting held regularly
to make and enforce laws, settle quarrels and decide on suitable punishment. This was
called a ‘folk moot' with the leading freemen of the tribe or village making the decisions.
As the population increased and dispersed throughout England, kingdoms were set
up, but it was not until the tenth century that the country was united under one ruler.
Distances made it impossible for all the freemen to assemble as in the older ‘folk moot' days,
and there gradually developed a simple form of representation of chosen men from each
district to regularly attend meetings. The group was called the 'Witan’, or the meeting of wise
men.
The main objectives of the Witan were to advise the King on matters of law-making,
the levying of taxes and the defence of the kingdom. All the Saxon rulers used the Witan
system, and, although it held little resemblance to the later developed parliamentary system,
it nevertheless created in the minds of the people the view that the King should not be an
absolute ruler.
With the invasion of England by William, Duke of Normandy, there were swift and
radical changes. The Witan was abolished and a Great Council was established, made up
of the great barons and leading churchmen. William was an autocratic ruler and called the
Great Council together quite infrequently. There remained, however, the strong feeling that
the Great Council should become an important voice of the people, so that Kings should rule
in the interests of all the King's subjects.

Dear Ms Alford,
Once again another sea rescue that was completely unnecessary has taken place.
Small craft, sailing vessels and helicopters have been involved in a four-day search of our
coastline, often in appalling weather and dangerous seas because of human stupidity.
| am very pleased that the Haslan family was finally rescued from the serious danger

The area outside Barr's Point is well known as a place where the current can run in the
opposite direction to the waves. When this happens the waves can overrun each other and

weather forecasts for fishermen and the general conditions north and south of Eastview are

the safety of the lives of their family.

October 1943
The desert night was almost over, the velvety darkness thinning to pink. At his post, Erich
glanced up, watching the foreign stars beginning to twinkle into obscurity.
“It is cold, yes?”
“Yes.” His companion was talkative. A private named Janz. Twenty-two or three years
old but still wet behind the ears, as far as Erich was concerned.
“You think they will come today?”
Erich shrugged a noncommittal reply. Who knew? Perhaps today, perhaps tomorrow.
Sometimes soon, that was certain.
“They say there are reinforcements on their way from the north.” His companion reached
for a cigarette. “Put that away, idiot! Do you want to bring the whole British army down on
us?”
“Sorry.” Janz’s fingers, numb with cold, fumbled the cigarettes back into his shirt pocket
and the silence of the desert settled again.
Erich stared into the growing dawn, watching the light slowly ooze along the landscape
and across the rolling dunes towards them as the invisible sun climbed towards the horizon.
“At least it will warm up soon, yes?”
“Yes. And then we will burn all day.”
It was the worst thing about this cursed desert — when it wasn’t freezing, it was boiling.
During the day the sun would blaze down on the little encampment, scorching pale
Germanic skin into angry red welts easily inflamed by the sand which seeped its way into
every crack and cranny of the body. It was bad enough that they were there, worse because
none of them had any idea why.
Excerpt from ‘Fireshadow’ by Anthony Eaton

Bird species threatened
WITH its habitat drying out fast, and no sign of rescue, the Australasian bittern needs a
miracle. Listed as critically endangered, it’s a heartbeat from extinction.
Also in trouble through wetlands neglect are the blue-billed duck, Lewins rail and the
Australian painted snipe.
Professor Stephen Garnett, chairman of Birds Australia’s threatened-birds committee,
says many Australian bird species had “coped with dry periods in the past ... waterfowl in
particular are highly mobile and able to travel from one wetland to another.
“But some of the core refuges in the southern part of the continent are drying out, and
that will leave some with nowhere to go.”
Professor Garnett described the wetland woes as “a failure of government and a failure
of the market in terms of water being counted as free goods for too long’.
In the Coorong wetlands in South Australia, the fairy tern has been left homeless and
pelicans no longer breed.
Closer to home, the Victorian Wetlands Network has been disbanded because of a lack
of funding — but founder Aidan Banfield has built wetlands on his Grampians property,
prompted by a decline in frog species.
While wetland species such as herons and snipes have visited Mr Banfield’s 30 ponds,
most of the visiting birds are woodland species seeking respite from the big dry.
JOHN ELDER
The Sunday Age

He lived in a tin hut with a hard dirt floor,
He had bags sewn together that was his door.

Looking for work though none could be found.

Yet he could not vote after his desert melée.

title: STT2024|STT31 ENG — Questions 14-20
passage:
H.M.S. BELLEROPHON
On June 1* 1815 an attempt was made by the French to break the blockade of Europe
imposed by the British navy. France under Napoleon had already conquered most of
Europe but was short of food. A convoy of American grain ships escorted by fleet of French
warships attempted to penetrate the blockade and unload at the French port of Brest. The
convoy was intercepted however by the British fleet commanded by Admiral Howe. A great
engagement ensued and for many hours the battles raged. Although some of the grain
ships managed to limp into harbour, eventually the British emerged as victors inflicting
heavy losses on the French.
One of the British warships participating in the battle was Bellerophon. With 74 guns,
Bellerophon, the flagship of the Fleet, was possibly the finest warship afloat at the time.
The ship was in the thick of the battle for some hours, taking a bad battering, and her
causalities included the captain, Rear Admiral Parsley, who lost a leg to a cannon shot. On
board Bellerophon at the time was a young officer, scarcely more than a boy, acting as
Aide-de-camp to the Admiral. His name was Mathew Flinders.
In between bouts of destruction caused by French broadsides and the noise and chaos
of the Bellerophon’s own guns being fired as the battle raged back and forth, Flinders was
able to find time to jot down notes on the course of the battle for the Admiral. This was one
of his official duties. The description in his journal, copied up at the end of the battle, runs
to 40 pages and is regarded by naval historians as the best account of this most famous
battle. From it they are able to judge exactly the course of the engagement.
Flinders survived the ‘Battle of the Glorious First’ and, at a later date of course, became
quite famous in a different way as a navigator and explorer although still serving as an
officer in the Royal Navy. The Bellerophon too lived on to carry out at least one more
famous voyage when she carried Napoleon from France to Portsmouth before he was
transported as a prisoner to the Island of St Helena in the Atlantic Ocean.

The New Teacher
Ellen had never lived so far out in the country. She’d been brought up near Melbourne,
where her parents owned a small grocery store. It had been a wrench to leave her
family and her friends to come here — but it was an adventure, too!
Well, she’d been in Jinderoo for more than a year, and the country way of life, at first so
strange, was now familiar and comfortable. She had learned to wear stout boots, to
save her washing water for the garden flowers, to rise earlier and go to bed sooner. She
boarded with a widow who had a spare room in her house, and who did her best to give

“My, you’re skinny,” she would remark sorrowfully, glancing at Ellen’s trim waist; and
Ellen would laugh, and eat another drop - scone thickly spread with butter, just to please
her.
Ellen’s predecessor in the schoolhouse had been Mr. Greg. The children, so used to
saying “Please, sir’, “Yes, sir’, “No, sir’, had found it difficult to get used to the idea of
saying “miss” instead. Hands were clapped to mouths in consternation each time the
mistake occurred, and an infectious giggle would ripple round the room.

Brumby’s Run
It lies beyond the Western Pines
Towards the sinking sun,
And not a survey mark defines
The bounds of “Brumby’s Run’.
On odds and ends of mountain land,
On tracks of range and rock
Where no one else can make a stand,
Old Brumby rears his stock.
Awild, unhandled lot they are
Of every shape and breed.
They venture out ‘neath moon and star
Along the flats to feed;
But when the dawn makes pink the sky
And steals along the plain,
The Brumby horses turn and fly
Towards the hills again.
The traveller by the mountain-track
May hear their hoof-beats pass,
And catch a glimpse of brown and black
Dim shadows on the grass.
The eager stockhorse pricks his ears
And lifts his head on high
In wild excitement when he hears
The Brumby mob go by.
Old Brumby asks no price or fee
O’er all his wide domains:
The man who yards his stock is free
To keep them for his pains.
So, off to:scour the mountain-side
With eager eyes aglow,
To strongholds where the wild mobs hide
The gully-rakers go.
Arush of horses through the trees,
A red shirt making play;
A sound of stockwhips on the breeze,
They vanish far away!
Ah, me! before our day is done
We long with bitter pain
To ride once more on Brumby’s Run
And yard his mob again.

passage:
READY TO RUMBLE!
by Dr Karl Kruszeinicki in Good Weekend, The Sydney Morning Herald Magazine, June
12, 2004.
Domestic cats have lived with people for many thousands of years. It’s a simple and
happy relationship — we take care of them, and they catch rodents for us. They let us
know that we have kept our side of the bargain by purring — a sure sign of contentment.
Or is it?
The sound of a cat's purr is very distinctive. It starts when they’re about a week old. They
can do it while either breathing in or breathing out, and with their mouths closed. If you
try, you can make a kind of rumble while you breathe out, but the rumble generated while
breathing in sounds rather strangled. Oddly, cats that purr (domestic cats, mountain lions,
pumas, etc.) can’t roar all that well, and cats that have a terrifying roar (tigers, lions, etc.)
aren’t too good at purring.
The mechanics of a cat’s purr are still a bit of a mystery. A cute version of a human’s
snore, perhaps? We now know that the cat’s throat emits short bursts of sound between
25 and 200 times each second. There’s a very short interruption to this regular pattern
as the cat changes from breathing in to breathing out, and vice versa. Over the years
there have been many theories, but the most popular one is that the pipe through which
the air passes to and from the cat’s lungs changes its diameter abruptly 25 to 200 times
each second. No one is quite sure where the change in diameter happens, or what drives
it, although it has been found that electrical signals change 25 to 200 times each seconds
in some of the muscles in the cat's air pipe.
So when do cats purr? Indeed, they do purr when they are contented, but they may also
purr when they are in pain, or giving birth, or being threatened.
A cat's purr is a bit like a human smile. Sure, we smile when we are happy, but we might
also smile nervously when we feel threatened, or if somebody is being catty towards us.
- Reading Skills page 1

title: STT2024|STT34 ENG — Questions 6-10
passage:
There are novel ways of getting teenage boys reading and girls
into IT, writes Blanche Clark
THE accepted wisdom is that boys and girls learn differently, but that doesn’t mean
educators are accepting gender differences as a fait accompli.
Moves are afoot to make reading as speccy as footy and computer games for adolescent
boys and IT as fabulous as fashion and social networking for girls.
Concern that boys are lagging behind girls in reading tests has led to numerous primary
and secondary programs.
But the State Library of Victoria’s Boys, Blokes, Books and Bytes program concentrates
on years 5-8, a period when many boys give up reading for pleasure.
Developed by the library’s Centre of Youth Literature, it promotes boys, their families,
schools and libraries talking about books.
The library’s reader development and onsite learning manager, Paula Kelly, says a toolkit
has been sent to every co-ed and boys’ school in Victoria. The program includes a website
with advice on great reads for boys and a blog for boys to discuss books.
“It's not so much that boys can’t read, as they choose not to read. They don’t see it as
cool and acceptable,” Kelly says.
“There’s also a distinct lack of male role models actually reading. When they see their
dads reading or other men reading it is usually for purposes of work. They equate the idea
of reading as work; it’s not fun.”
Schools are encouraged to run boys’ book clubs, invite fathers and other male role
models to the school and form partnerships with local libraries.
Kelly says boys need a choice about what they read, and novels, non-fiction, graphic
novels, books that have an audio component, and comics should all be offered.
“Sure reading a novel raises your chances of school achievement, but ultimately reading
is good for you; it’s about your wellbeing.”
She says the library is often asked if it will offer a similar program for girls.
“Girls come to reading much more easily. No one looks at a girl and goes, ‘You're a bit of
nerd because you're a reader’. There is no issue with girls, but there is with boys.”
At the launch of the program on Thursday, University of Melbourne vice chancellor Prof
Glyn Davis said the program was a positive way to encourage children to read without
getting bogged down in political debates about methods of teaching literacy.
“There are important things about cultural literacy and basic reading skills in this program,
but the end result is designed to get boys reading and to enjoy reading,” he said.
Davis said it was hard to explain why it had become difficult to encourage boys to read.
“But a key part of the explanation lies in the electronic world and all the current
alternatives to books,” he said.
Herald-Sun October 14 2008

title: STT2024|STT34 ENG — Questions 11-17
passage:
Descent from the Summit
by John Murray.
Simon felt the temperature dropping on the summit. For the first time, the sun disappeared
completely, plunging them into a dusky gloom. Simon knew that they did not have any
more time. He was not sure how fit Brechner was, but knew that they would have to go,
and take a chance. He didn’t have to speak to Gilbert. “Going. Going now,” Gilbert said,
lumbering over to the edge.
They shortened the safety lines to twenty feet. Gilbert was the lead and they put Brechner
between him and Simon. Between them, he reasoned, they would be able to hold him if he
slipped. “Happy birthday, Brechner,” Simon said as they pulled on their oxygen masks
again and stopped speaking. Simon knew that he had to find a rhythm and concentrate on
the ground in front of him. He was thinking too much about Brechner. He was too anxious,
too eager to get down. Climbers killed climbers, he knew. It was the thin air, the tiredness,
and the cold that were doing it to him. He took long deep breaths of oxygen. He checked
his gloves and jackets again and tried to relax his abdomen and calves. And then he
lumbered around and eased himself back off the edge after Gilbert and Brechner. Simon
heard the metallic rattle of pegs and clips around Gilbert's waist as he lowered himself
down the slope ahead of him.
They descended down the buttress and were moving along the first ridge when the cold
front hit them. The wind picked up to a steady fifteen Knots and walls of cloud began
blowing over the mountain. The air filled with curtains of grey fog. The cloud in front of
Simon’s face was wispy and glutinous. Ahead of him, he saw the dark form of Brechner,
hunched forward, walking with wide swings of his arms. The safety line was limp between
them and lay on the snow like a crack on a white cement wall. Simon could still just make
out Gilbert up front, walking smoothly and with long high steps down the incline. Their
footholds were still clearly visible in the snow, and Simon concentrated on placing his
boots in the centre of each to minimise his effort and to reduce the chance of slipping. He
felt the muscles in his forehead clenching. His eyes were dry and gritty. Simon knew that
they would need about an hour to traverse this top ridge, which angled to the south. It was
most vulnerable they would be on the descent. He imagined the three of them in his mind
as bobbing specks, like currants swirling in milk.

By John Foulcher
Accrab, spurting from the water,
dangling its legs over shells. It lugs its body
sideways, like a survivor dragged clear,

passage:
A Good Woman (2005)
Reviewed by Neil Smith PG
Updated 08 May 2005 Contains mild language and sex references
Recent film versions of The Importance Of Being Earnest and An Ideal Husband have
faithfully retained Oscar Wilde's view of snobbish 19th-century society. Kudos, then, to A
Good Woman helmer Mike Barker for moving Wilde's play Lady Windermere's Fan to 1930s
Italy, where the author's pithy aphorisms compete for our attention with gorgeous
Mediterranean scenery. The dialogue proves a mouthful for society gals Helen Hunt and
Scarlett Johansson, so Tom Wilkinson shines brightest as an ageing toff with a heart of gold.
Hunt plays Mrs Erlynne, a penniless New York socialite who travels to Europe to squeeze
cash out of young newlyweds Robert and Meg Windermere (Mark Umbers and Scarlett
Johansson) and find herself a new man. The notorious seductress is soon enjoying secret
liaisons with Robert while Meg, convinced that her new husband is having an affair, falls into
the arms of the caddish Lord Darlington (Bright Young Things’ Stephen Campbell Moore).
"SKILLFULLY BANISHES THEATRICALITY“
Wilde's 1892 play was his first stage success and set the template for his other studies of
class and human nature. But while Barker keeps faith with the author's classy wit and
waspish repartee, he skillfully banishes theatricality by taking the action out of the salon and
into the bustling beauty of the Amalfi coast. The result may be reminiscent of The Talented
Mr Ripley and A Room With A View, but it's still a classy diversion that, like Bright Young
Things before it, evokes a bygone age of deliciously divine decadence.

title: STT2024|STT38 ENG — Questions 11-15
passage:
ANCIENT MURDER MYSTERY SOLVED?
TUTANKHAMEN was only ten years old when he became the Pharaoh of Egypt around
3300 years ago. The cause of his death, at a young age, has been an enduring mystery
that has puzzled historians, archaeologists, forensic scientists and even police detectives
ever since his mummified body was uncovered in 1922.
The discovery of Tutankhamen’s tomb fuelled speculation about the possible cause of his
death. Unlike most other Egyptian tombs, although the antechamber and annex had been
disturbed, Tutankhamen’s burial chamber had been untouched by tomb raiders or vandals.
It was filled with fabulous treasures, including a priceless gold funeral mask. However the
tomb was small and clearly unfinished in parts, which gave rise to the theory that the
young pharaoh had died suddenly and the tomb had been hastily prepared. This led
experts to surmise that Tutankhamen had been murdered.
Tutankhamen’s mummy was first examined by Dr Douglas Derry. Derry established that
the king had been about eighteen when he died. In 1963 Tutankhamen’s body was x-rayed
by R.G.Harrison, an anatomist and an authority on mummies. The x-ray revealed a
possible skull fracture suggesting that Tutankhamen may have been killed by a blow to the
back of the head. This finding was strongly supported by further tests in the mid-1990s
which led to a hunt for a long-dead murderer.
Bob Brier, a researcher from Long Island University and two former US police officers,
Greg Cooper and Mike King, were just some of the people who became obsessed with
identifying King Tutankhamen’s killer. Using modern forensic and profiling techniques they
began their own investigation. There were several suspects: Ay, Tutankhamen’s chief
adviser who succeeded him as Pharaoh; Maya, his treasurer; Horemheb, his general who
also became Pharaoh after Ay’s death; and Ankhesenamen, Tutankhamen’s wife, who
later named Ay. The investigator agreed that Ay had the most to gain from Tutankhamen’s
death and felt satisfied that they had correctly identified the ancient assassin. However,
many Egyptologists remained skeptical and subsequent tests have suggested a
completely new scenario: King Tutankhamen may have died from an infection in a badly
broken leg.
Aresearch team, led by Zahi Hawass, the Chairman of Egypt's Supreme Council of
Antiquities, examined images of the mummy taken from a CT scan and concluded that
there was no evidence of a blow to the back of the head, and therefore no indication of foul
play. The most recent theory that Tutankhamen died as a result of a broken leg may help
to solve another, smaller mystery: why, among the glorious treasures in Tutankhamen’s
tomb, there were also 130 walking sticks!

Wealth data tells a tale of two cities
Tim Colebatch
TWO towers symbolise the gap between affluence and deprivation in Melbourne. Barely
three kilometres apart, fringing the city in opposite directions, the 2006 Census shows them
as polar opposites of socio-economic advantage and disadvantage in our state.
The desirable tower is Yarra’s Edge, the award-winning "urban village" developed by Mirvac
on the old site of South Wharf, in Docklands. On a wide-ranging index of measures, the
Bureau of Statistics ranks it the most socioeconomically advantaged community in Victoria.
The tough tower is an old Housing Commission block of flats, on the corner of Melrose and
Canning Streets in North Melbourne, down from Racecourse Road. Many of its residents
are refugees, Islam is the main religion, and only 39 people have a job.
From census data collected in more than 9000 districts throughout Victoria, the Bureau has
constructed an index of socioeconomic advantage and disadvantage, ranking each district
— ranging in size from city blocks to large areas of farmland and forest — from 1 to 9055.
The index covers 21 variables, such as the proportion of households with high or low
incomes, the proportion with broadband or no internet access, how many people work as
professionals or labourers, the size of mortgages and rent payments, the number of
bedrooms, and occupants' qualifications.
At both ends, the extremes are clustered in towers edging the city. Six of the 10 most
advantaged districts are new apartment blocks in Docklands, Southbank, Port Melbourne
and the CBD. And nine of the 10 most disadvantaged are old Housing Commission towers
in North Melbourne, Ascot Vale, Kensington and Collingwood.
One difference leaps out: at the Melrose Street flats, only 25% of people were born in
Australia, as against 65% at Yarra's Edge. And, at Yarra's Edge, the migrants come mostly
from the US, Malaysia and England; at Melrose Street, from Vietnam, China, Somalia and
Eritrea.
While tax data last week showed the taxman still makes his biggest hauls in Portsea, Toorak,
and Brighton, the Bureau's index, finds the new towers along the Yarra and the waterfront
have Melbourne's greatest concentration of well-off people.
The second best collection of Melburnians lives in Southbank just behind the National
Gallery. Southbank and Docklands each have two collectors’ districts in the top 10, which
also include Beacon Cove in Port Melbourne (sixth) and the city block bounded by La Trobe,
Queen, Lonsdale and William streets.

“Dream on Cedar” text from The Slightly True Story of Cedar B. Hartley
by Martine Murray.
There’s a long way between an idea and a real thing. Inside your mind there is a boundless
view. You can imagine whatever you want.
For example, you can plan exactly how you would like your house to be.
You close your eyes and picture spiral staircases with slippery banisters and blue wooden
floors and stars stuck on the ceilings, and a grass carpet for rabbits in the rabbit room.
Sometimes there might be a white cow on the couch or a herd of wild wandering albatrosses,
wearing new hats and recently returned all the way from Russia to tell you tales, waiting in
your bathtub which is a big as a bus and always perfectly warm with honey-scented bubbles.
And through the diamond shapes on the windows, all you can see is every kind of tree, even
mountain ash, and some with swinging ropes and the warbling of lemon-bellied fly ~ catchers
and laughing kookaburras and some festooned with rare spotted birds that sing like Stevie
Wonder.
And then, just at the moment when you're in the trees swinging from a rope and going all
Tarzan, your mum yells out and you have to open your eyes. ‘Cedar! Dinner’s ready.’
So you open them, and lo and behold, there you are just lying on your back facing the
cracked ceiling above you.
That’s how it really is. Real life is a bit like a used tea towel. And you can’t get even one
single albatross to wear a hat and tell you tales in the bath, no matter what you do. Some
ideas just have to remain as ideas.

‘Hang Loose’ youth keep options open
(S1) Hugh Mackay is a social commentator and journalist who writes articles for the
Weekend Australian and the Sydney Morning Herald newspapers. He is a social researcher,
author and newspaper columnist.
lf you are looking for a symbol of contemporary youth culture, look no further than the laces
left untied on Doc Martens shoes. It’s as if the kids are saying, ‘I’m prepared to wear these
things, but | wouldn’t want you to think | was totally committed to the idea.’ As usual, the
rising generation are sending us a message from our future, so we’d better listen.
($2) Australians born since the mid-70s don’t share their parents’ and grandparents’ anxiety
about the rapid rate of change and its destabilising effect on our society. For them, constant
change is the air they breathe, the water they swim in. It is simply the way the world is. They
are the generation for whom the women’s movement was an established historical fact; the
generation who take equality between the sexes for granted (and who are infuriated by older
people — especially older men in senior positions — who still don’t understand that
personhood is a gender- neutral concept, and still haven’t grasped the essential difference
between yesterday's view of women and today’s). They know that more than 50 per cent of
university students are women, that 45 per cent (and rising) of the workforce are female and
that girls can do anything they choose. They know that most mothers have paid work outside
the home because that’s how it is for their own mothers. They don’t expect Mum to be there
making peanut butter sandwiches when they get home from school, and they vaguely
wonder why she even bothers mentioning the fact that that’s what her mother used to do.
($3) On the other hand, roughly 750,000 members of this generation live in a household
where no one is currently earning any wages, so the reality of unemployment is pretty stark.
Even if their parents have work, at least 30 per cent of young Australians are facing the bleak
prospect of a labour market that doesn’t want them . . . at least not yet. (If you had applied
unsuccessfully for 200 jobs, as a respondent in one of my recent research projects had,
what would you do next?)
(S4) To older Australians, the sharp rise in the divorce rate over the past 20 years seems
cataclysmic, shaking the very foundations of the institution of marriage. But to the rising
generation, nothing has changed: from the time they became aware of the nature of
marriage and divorce, they had known that lots of their friends live with one parent, so what’s
the big deal? Do you imagine that contemporary children and adolescents exchange
information about their parents’ marital status in darkly whispered confessions behind their
hands? Do you think that living in a one-parent family feels like a heavy burden for kids to
bear? Think again: almost one million dependent children are in precisely that situation,
which doesn’t mean that it’s always fun for them, but it does mean that it’s hardly worth
mentioning. (In any case, having one parent at home might sometimes feel like half the
burden of having two.) To the intense irritation of their parents, the members of this
generation are able to program the VCR without even reading the manual. Having grown up
in the thick of the information revolution (‘What revolution?’) they know today’s technology
is already obsolete by the time they get their hands on it, and that smarter things are
constantly coming over the horizon. They know there’s an accessible drug culture in every
town and suburb, and that ‘street kids’ are part of the scene. (No wonder they’ve embraced
the gritty realism of the new writing for young people.)
($5) Paradoxically, they’re also our most dependent generation, staying at home for longer
and relying on social security in larger numbers than any previous group of young
Australians. Like every generation before them, they are responding to the world as they
find it. (To what other world could they possibly respond?) Not surprisingly, their experience
of impermanence and unpredictability has taught them one big, central lesson: keep your
options open. So they are inclined to hang loose; to postpone commitment to a career, a
sexual partner, a political party, a set of religious beliefs, a brand . . . or even to whether
they'll be home for dinner tonight. For many of them, that is an exciting, liberating approach
to life. Those flapping shoelaces can be a sign of confidence, freedom, flexibility and
adaptability. But not for all: the lack of a clear focus and the absence of a stable framework
can also breed insecurity, uncertainty and an aching sense of alienation. In the wait-and-see
world of the young, even the symbol of untied laces is ambiguous.
By Hugh Mackay

Half-Truths
Beware of those who use the truth to deceive. When someone tells you something
that is true, but leaves out important information that should be included, he can
create a false impression.
For example, someone might say, “I just won a hundred dollars on the lottery. It
was great. | took that dollar ticket back to the store and turned it in for one hundred
dollars!”
This guy’s a winner, right? Maybe, maybe not. We then discover that he bought
two hundred tickets, and only one was a winner. He’s really a big loser!
He didn’t say anything that was false, but he deliberately omitted important
information. That’s called a half-truth. Half-truths are not technically lies, but they
are just as dishonest.
Untrustworthy candidates in political campaigns often use this tactic. Let’s say that
during Governor Smith’s last term, her state lost one million jobs and gained three
million jobs. Then she seeks another term. One of her opponents runs an ad
saying, “During Governor Smith’s term, the state lost one million jobs!” that’s true.
However an honest statement would have been, During Governor Smith’s term,
the state had a net gain of two million jobs.”

URANUS
Uranus, the seventh planet from the Sun, enjoys two distinct and long seasons. Forty-
two years of sunlight is followed by forty-two years of darkness. The reason for this is
that the planet, rings and moons are all tilted at an angle of 98 degrees, while other
planets look like spinning tops as they make their journey around the Sun, Uranus is
flipped on its side, and appears to be rolling around the Sun. Scientists do not have a
definite answer for why the planet lies in this way, but one reason postulated is a collision
with some other heavy body many millennia ago.
Uranus can be just barely seen with the naked eye, but it was not until it was examined
by telescope, that it was identified as a planet. This happened in 1781, when Sir William
Herschel found it while mapping the constellation of Gemini. Its faint ring system was
not discovered until 1977. There are eleven rings in total. It was once thought that
Uranus only had five moons: Miranda, Ariel, Umbriel, Titania and Oberon, but Voyager
Two along with various other telescopes revealed at least twenty-two new bodies. All
the moons revolve around the plane of the planet’s equator.
Uranus, rotates on its axis in about seventeen hours. The atmosphere is made up of
83% hydrogen, 15% helium and 2% methane. It is this methane which gives the planet
its characteristic blue appearance. The actual planet is composed of a solid rock
fragments that are up to a meter thick. This rock is some of the densest material ever
encountered in the universe.

ELEMENTS OF THE AUSTRALIAN FLAG
THE UNION JACK
The Australian national flag has the Union Jack in the upper left-hand quarter nearest the
flagpole (‘canton’) and the rest of the background (the ‘field’) coloured dark blue. The Union
Jack, the commonly used name for the Union flag, is the flag of the United Kingdom and has
its own history.
The first Union flag was created in 1606 and consisted of the red cross of St George
(England) on a white background and the white diagonal cross of St Andrew (Scotland) on
a dark blue background. This flag was first raised in Australia on 29 April 1770 by Captain
Cook at Stingray Harbour (later renamed Botany Bay). Cook raised it again at Possession
Island, off Cape York when he claimed the east coast of Australia in the name of King George
the Third. Governor Phillip hoisted this flag again on 26 January 1788 at Sydney Cove,
marking the first European settlement. ,
When Ireland became a part of the United Kingdom in 1801, the red
diagonal cross of St Patrick was added to the Union Jack. This flag Mw AA
was flown by European settlers and explorers across Australia until
Federation in 1901, when the Commonwealth of Australia was ie | bw
formed and the Australia national flag flew.
THE COMMONWEALTH STAR
The Commonwealth Star on the Australian national flag created in 1901
had six points representing the States (formerly colonies); the seventh point
was added in 1908 to represent Commonwealth Territories. Another reason
for this change was for the star to match the crest of the Commonwealth
Coat of Arms, the first version of which was created in 1908. The
Commonwealth Star is sometimes referred to as the Federation Star.
THE SOUTHERN CROSS
Four seven-pointed stars arranged in a cross, together with a smaller five-pointed star
appear on the right-hand side (‘fly’) of the flag to represent the Southern Cross. The
Southern Cross is a constellation that can be seen only in the night skies of the Southern
Hemisphere. It was a common feature of many of the early unofficial Australia flags. The
formal name of the Southern Cross is Crux Australis and the individual stars are named by
the first five letters of the Greek alphabet in order of brightness—{clockwise from the bottom
star) Alpha, Beta, Gamma, Delta and Epsilon.
The original competition-winning design had each star with a different *
number of points, ranging from nine to five to reflect their brightness. The *
number of points was simplified by the British Admiralty, and the official ¥*
x
drawing in the Commonwealth of Australia Gazette of 23 February 1903
showed the four larger stars of the same size with seven points each and *
the smaller one with five.
From ‘Australian Flags’ 1998

POKEMANIACS can attest that the urge to “catch’em all” in some games can be irresistible.
Yet while Spectrobes has strong instant appeal, this fossil-fuelled sequel still does not have
the same long-term allure as Nintendo’s pocket monster series.
Youngsters again guide a cocky young space cadet who can command Spectrobes, the
only creatures that can save the universe from a powerful new threat that can consume
entire planets. The critters are found in fossils deep underground, requiring trainers to
excavate, awaken and evolve them before they can be useful in battle.
Newcomers will initially enjoy the process of scouring planets for precious underground
booty, then carefully chipping away layers of rock, sand, lava and ice using the touch screen
while harnessing tools such as drills and vacuums to remove the treasure without shattering
its precious contents. The procedure can be tense and exciting, but eventually becomes a
tiresome chore as repetition sets in.
There are 185 Spectrobes to collect. While they still lack the charismatic charm of
Pokemon, it is fun to discover new creatures because of their unique attacks. Work has been
invested in the battle system, which remains simple and cumbersome but now offers some
much-needed depth.
Two Spectrobes are taken into each scuffle and players can instantly switch between
them. Unfortunately, players will struggle to always get the best view of the action as they
try to quickly pummel foes using melee and projectile-based attacks.
Although the rock-paper-scissors dynamic does little to prevent trainers from using the
same warriors every time, incubators encourage the development of a diverse squad. Mined
minerals can be fed to the creatures to improve their combat skills, rewarding those who
invest significant time in scavenger hunts. The game also supports multi-player battles and

Magna Carta
During the period 1100 to 1300 there were actions taken that contributed to the
development of the Westminster system of government. There had been a token _
parliament previously, where the King set up a Great Council to give advice on matters of
taxation, governance and national security. Quite frequently the Kings chose to act
completely autocratically and paid only lip service to the advice of this small but powerful
group of nobles and bishops.
It was this total disregard of the Great Council that brought about a situation,
where there was great unrest in England. King John took no heed of laws that had been
promulgated, and increased taxes without recourse to discussions with the Great Council.
The barons and the bishops were incensed by the King's conduct and acting on the advice
of the Archbishop of Canterbury, determined to force the King to rule justly. A famous
document was drawn up and King John was forced to sign this first great charter of English
liberty.
Although the document benefited most by the terms of Magna Carta, it led to
further extensions of rights and responsibilities for the common people. It contained three
very significant clauses, which even today are a cornerstone of our legal and governmental
system.
e No man shall be imprisoned except by the lawful judgement of his equals.
° To none shall justice be sold, denied or delayed.
These two clauses were included to ensure that persons could not be imprisoned on the
whim of a king, and that there must be an honest and accountable justice system.
@ The King shall impose no tax without the consent of the Great Council.
Although later kings did not always honour these three clauses, it was the beginning of an
era where the monarchy ruled through a parliamentary system that empowered the
citizens of England to have some input into the governance of the country.

Imagine you are back in the eighteenth century, without the benefit of modern

transported. Some cattle, pigs, horses, sheep and plant seeds will be obtained at

This then was the task of the founder of the first European settlement in Australia,
Captain Arthur Phillip. He was appointed to this task in 1776. This energetic, colonial
administrator began his task with great enthusiasm, and, such was his ability and his
superb organisational skills, that he managed to overcome a list of difficulties that would
have broken a Jesser man. The settlement was made at Sydney Cove in 1788.

caused by the unwillingness of the authorities in England to pay sufficient attention to

aspects. The officers were frequently quarrelsome and did not often display a diligent
attitude to what was a monumental task. To add to this list, problems arose with the
indigenous population despite Phillips’ attempts to keep the peace. Food was in short

We return to Captain Haldane and his friends, who had been meditating escape from the
first day of their arrival at the Staats Model School. The difficulty was, of course, the
guards, and Mr. Churchill's exploit made the Boer Government redouble its vigilance. It
was found impossible to bribe the sentries; a plan for a rising of the prisoners was soon
given up; and the scheme of sinking a shaft and then tunnelling to an adjacent kitchen
garden proved impracticable, since the diggers very soon struck water. For three miserable
months Captain Haldane cogitated in vain, and the best he could do was to get hold of a
tourist map of South Africa and study the country east of Pretoria in case some way of
escape should present itself. Meantime an incident cheered the prisoners. A man
accompanied by a St. Bernard dog took to walking outside the school and signalling by the
Morse code with his stick. He was warned off by the guards, but he found another means
of communication and sent messages from an adjacent house giving the news of the war.
In the middle of February 1900 there was a rumour that the officers were to be moved to a
new building from which escape would be impossible. This gave Captain Haldane an idea.
He resolved to go into hiding beneath the floor, so that the Boers should think he had
escaped, and then, when the officers were moved and the building was left empty, to
emerge and get out of the town. His companions in the attempt were Lieutenant Neil Le
Mesurier of the Dublin Fusiliers and Sergeant-Major A. Brockie of the Imperial Light Horse.
They collected a few necessary articles, opened the trap-door, and went to earth.
It was a horrible place in which they found themselves. The floor of the building was about
2 feet above the ground, and the space below was divided into five narrow compartments
by four stone walls, on which the cross beams rested. Each of these compartments was
about 18 feet long and 30 feet wide, and there were manholes between them. The air,
what there was of it, came through a small ventilator somewhere on the veranda. The
place was pitch dark, and the atmosphere was stuffy to the last degree. The three thought
that their imprisonment there would only last for twenty-four hours. They went to earth on
26th February, and next day there was a great to-do about their disappearance.
Descriptions of them were circulated over the whole country. One of their friends above,
Lieutenant Frankland of the Dublin Fusiliers, arranged a small daily supply of provisions.

Hating Alison Ashley (PG)
By Sandra Hall
March 19, 2005, Sydney Morning Herald
It's a girls' world in this comic and colourful adaptation of a-much-loved children's novel,
writes Sandra Hall.
Directed by Geoff Bennett
Screenplay by Christine Madafferi form the novel by Robin Klein
Rated PG
Cinemas Everywhere
It should come as no surprise that Delta Goodrem doesn't convince as a 14-year-old
schoolgirl. Hiding under a Mona Lisa smile and a Goldilocks wig, she looks like a 20-year-
old pop star on the run from the paparazzi.
Not that it matters: The film of Hating Alison Ashley, Robin Klein's much-read children's novel
has little to do with the real world. It's set in Ockerdom, a place where we patriotic filmgoers
have spent a lot of time lately, thanks to the run of comedies which have been trying, with
raucous relentlessness, to make themselves loveable in the happy-go-lucky manner of The
Castle.
Hating Alison Ashley is not really Alison's story. As Klein's many fans know, its narrator is
_ Alison's classmate, Erica Yurken (Saskia Burmeister), a talented self-dramatist, who fancies
she's been stranded in the wrong life. Her refined sensibilities, she thinks, are more suited
to some ivy-covered temple of learning than scungy, working-class Barringa East, where
she's been dumped among the delinquents of 9C. Whenever she can, she escapes to the
sick bay, where her impressive list of imaginary ailments has gained her a reputation as a
creative hypochondriac.
And life at home is no better. Although her sweet-natured mum (Tracy Mann) does her best,
Erica can't forgive her for taking up with Lennie (Richard Carter), a truck driver she met at
Parents Without Partners, or for giving her such unbearable siblings. Her chief torturer is her
elder sister, boy-mad Valjoy (Rachael Carpani), whose boots and big hair are almost as
scary as her interest in martial arts.
School improves for Erica with the arrival of Miss Belmont (Jean Kittson), whose fishnet
stockings and gallows humour give her the air of a semi-respectable dominatrix. Miss
Belmont does the previously unthinkable and keeps 9C in order. She also gives Erica high
marks and makes her feel special - until the arrival of Goodrem's Alison Ashley.
Alison is perfection incarnate. For a minute or two, Erica fancies she has found a kindred
spirit. But Alison proves to be strangely aloof. And, even worse, the quality of her classwork
eclipses Erica's.

H.M.S. BELLEROPHON
On June 1% 1815 an attempt was made by the French to break the blockade of Europe
imposed by the British navy. France under Napoleon had already conquered most of
Europe but was short of food. A convoy of American grain ships escorted by fleet of French
warships attempted to penetrate the blockade and unload at the French port of Brest. The
convoy was intercepted however by the British fleet commanded by Admiral Howe. A great
engagement ensued and for many hours the battles raged. Although some of the grain
ships managed to limp into harbour, eventually the British emerged as victors inflicting
heavy losses on the French.
One of the British warships participating in the battle was Bellerophon. With 74 guns,
Bellerophon, the flagship of the Fleet, was possibly the finest warship afloat at the time.
The ship was in the thick of the battle for some hours, taking a bad battering, and her
causalities included the captain, Rear Admiral Parsley, who lost a leg to a cannon shot. On
board Bellerophon at the time was a young officer, scarcely more than a boy, acting as
Aide-de-camp to the Admiral. His name was Mathew Flinders.
In between bouts of destruction caused by French broadsides and the noise and chaos
of the Bellerophon’s own guns being fired as the battle raged back and forth, Flinders was
able to find time to jot down notes on the course of the battle for the Admiral. This was one
of his official duties. The description in his journal, copied up at the end of the battle, runs
to 40 pages and is regarded by naval historians as the best account of this most famous
battle. From it they are able to judge exactly the course of the engagement.
Flinders survived the ‘Battle of the Glorious First’ and, at a later date of course, became
quite famous in a different way as a navigator and explorer although still serving as an
officer in the Royal Navy. The Bellerophon too lived on to carry out at least one more
famous voyage when she carried Napoleon from France to Portsmouth before he was
transported as a prisoner to the Island of St Helena in the Atlantic Ocean.

READY TO RUMBLE!
by Dr Karl Kruszelnicki in Good Weekend, The Sydney Morning Herald Magazine, June
12, 2004.
Domestic cats have lived with people for many thousands of years. It’s a simple and
happy relationship — we take care of them, and they catch rodents for us. They let us
know that we have kept our side of the bargain by purring — a sure sign of contentment.
Or is it?
The sound of a cat’s purr is very distinctive. It starts when they're about a week old. They
can do it while either breathing in or breathing out, and with their mouths closed. If you
try, you can make a kind of rumble while you breathe out, but the rumble generated while
breathing in sounds rather strangled. Oddly, cats that purr (domestic cats, mountain lions,
pumas, etc.) can’t roar all that well, and cats that have a terrifying roar (tigers, lions, etc.)
aren't too good at purring.
The mechanics of a cat’s purr are still a bit of a mystery. A cute version of a human’s
snore, perhaps? We now know that the cat’s throat emits short bursts of sound between
25 and 200 times each second. There’s a very short interruption to this regular pattern
as the cat changes from breathing in to breathing out, and vice versa. Over the years
there have been many theories, but the most popular one is that the pipe through which
the air passes to and from the cat’s lungs changes its diameter abruptly 25 to 200 times
each second. No one is quite sure where the change in diameter happens, or what drives
it, although it has been found that electrical signals change 25 to 200 times each seconds
in some of the muscles in the cat’s air pipe.
So when do cats purr? Indeed, they do purr when they are contented, but they may also
purr when they are in pain, or giving birth, or being threatened.
A cat's purr is a bit like a human smile. Sure, we smile when we are happy, but we might
also smile nervously when we feel threatened, or if somebody is being catty towards us.

ICE SPIKES
Dr Alice Caseleyr 2005.
What are ice spikes?
Ice spikes are unusual structures that occasionally grow out of the ice cube trays in your
freezer. They look like the limestone stalagmites that are sometimes found in caves.
How do ice spikes form?
Ice spikes grow as the water in an ice cube tray turns to ice. Beginning on the top of each
cube, the water freezes inwards until only a small hole is left unfrozen in the centre. At
the same time as the surface solidifies, ice also starts to form under it, at the sides and
on the bottom of the cube. Since water expands as it freezes, the ice forming below the
hardened surface starts to push some water up through the hole. This water begins to
form the ice spike’s tubular shape. As water continues to be pushed out, it travels up the
tube, freezing around the rim and adding to its length. The spike will continue growing
until all the water in the cube becomes frozen of until the mouth of the tube ices over. Ice
spikes have been known to grow to a length of 56mm.
What helps ice spikes grow?
Experiments show that spikes are more likely to form when distilled water is used in the
trays and the temperature is just below freezing point (0° Celsius). If the temperature is
too low, the ice cube will freeze solid before the tube can begin to grow. Ice spikes will
also form more often if a fan is installed in the freezer to circulate the air. This is because
the moving air cools the top of the ice cube more rapidly. At the optimum temperature,
and with air blowing over the ice tray, approximately half of the cubes should develop ice
spikes.

Extract A: New Caledonia — A French Paradise in the South Pacific
New Caledonia is a French territory in the South Pacific. It is a magnificent group of islands
about four hours by air from Australia. Spectacular coral reefs, glistening blue-green
lagoons and palm-fringed areas make for an idyllic tourist destination. While the main
airport is located at the northern end of the island, the capital city, Nouméa, is positioned
some ninety minutes away at the southern extremity. The largest island is known as Grand
Terre. There are many spectacular islands and cays with pristine beaches of shimmering
white sand.
_The islands have a fascinating mix of two cultures; the French, who colonised the territory
in 1853, and the Kanaks, the indigenous Melanesian inhabitants. There are more than 300
tribes in New Caledonia and these are organised into large groups of families ruled over by
a chief.
For the tourists, there are fascinating and exciting areas to visit and enjoy. The Isle of
Pines, a half-hour flight from Nouméa, the capital city, has a number of beautifully
appointed bungalows on the beach with a resort-style hotel and facilities. The exquisite
palms form a backdrop to the dazzling azure-blue of the lagoons in the immediate area.
Sites such as the convict ruins of Nouville remind the visitor of the days when French
political prisoners were transported to New Caledonia. The Jean-Marie Tjibaou Cultural
Centre was set up in the 1990s to showcase the history and culture of the Kanak people.
There has been a move towards gradual independence since 1998. The impact of French
colonialism has irrevocably shaped the region. The fusion of the two French and Kanak
cultures makes for a fascinating mix and ensures that New Caledonia is an engaging
tourist destination.
Extract B: Fiji — The Heart of the South Pacific
Fiji is a tropical paradise located in the South Pacific, known for its stunning beaches,
crystal-clear waters, and vibrant marine life. Comprising over 330 islands, Fiji is a cultural
and natural wonderland. The two largest islands, Viti Levu and Vanua Levu, are home to
most of the population, with the capital city, Suva, located on Viti Levu. Fiji is a favourite
destination for honeymooners, adventure seekers, and families alike.
The islands boast some of the world’s most pristine coral reefs, making snorkelling and
scuba diving popular activities. Visitors are drawn to places like the Yasawa and
Mamanuca island chains, known for their white sandy beaches and turquoise lagoons.
Cultural sites, such as traditional Fijian villages, offer a glimpse into the rich heritage of the
indigenous iTaukei people, who have lived on the islands for over 3,000 years. Firewalking
ceremonies, kava rituals, and Meke performances are essential parts of the Fijian
experience.
Fiji became a British colony in 1874 and gained independence in 1970. The influence of
British colonialism remains evident, especially in the architecture and legal system.
However, Fiji’s culture is firmly rooted in its indigenous traditions, creating a unique blend
of old and new. Fiji's warmth extends beyond its tropical climate, with the Fijian people
renowned for their friendliness and hospitality, making every visitor feel at home.

Extract A: Gibraltar: The Strategic Sentinel of the Mediterranean
Gibraltar is situated at the southern tip of the Iberian Peninsula, bordering Spain, and
encompasses an area of approximately five square kilometres. Despite its modest size,
Gibraltar holds immense strategic importance, commanding the western entrance to the
Mediterranean Sea. This pivotal location has rendered Gibraltar a coveted prize
throughout history, making it the focal point of numerous sieges and military campaigns.
The narrow Strait of Gibraltar serves as the gateway between the Atlantic Ocean and the
Mediterranean, making control of this area crucial for naval dominance and trade routes.
After the Moors were expelled from Spain in the late 15th century, the territory remained
under Spanish control for several centuries. The rugged terrain, dominated by the iconic
Rock of Gibraltar, provided a formidable defence against invaders, allowing the Spanish to
maintain their hold despite external pressures. However, the strategic value of Gibraltar
could not be overlooked by other European powers.
The turning point came during the War of the Spanish Succession in the early 18th
century. In 1704, an Anglo-Dutch fleet seized Gibraltar from Spain, marking the beginning
of British involvement in the region. This military manoeuvre was part of a broader conflict
over the Spanish throne, and control of Gibraltar provided the British with a critical naval
base. The Treaty of Utrecht in 1713 formally ceded Gibraltar to Great Britain, solidifying its
status as a British Overseas Territory. Since then, Gibraltar has remained under British
administration, despite periodic attempts by Spain to reclaim it. In 1967, the people of
Gibraltar exercised their right to self-determination by voting overwhelmingly to retain their
connection with Great Britain. This referendum was a decisive moment in Gibraltar's
history, reinforcing the population's desire to remain British amidst ongoing disputes with
Spain over sovereignty.
Extract B: The Suez Canal: An Essential Artery of Global Trade
From its inception, the Suez Canal has been a linchpin in global commerce, by connecting
the Mediterranean Sea to the Red Sea it serves as a vital artery for the transportation of
oil, natural gas, and a myriad of other commodities. Bypassing the lengthy route around
the south of Africa, the canal provides a direct route between Europe and Asia. Major
shipping lines traverse the canal daily, accounting for approximately 10% of all global
trade. The efficiency and reliability of the Suez Canal continues to underpin global supply
chains, making it a cornerstone of modern trade.
The canal, however, has been a focal point of geopolitical tensions since its construction. It
was initially under French and Egyptian control, but British involvement soon followed due
to its significance for trade and military strategy. During the 1956 Suez Crisis, Egypt
nationalised the canal, leading to a military intervention by Britain, France, and Israel.
Although military intervention temporarily disrupted canal operations, international
pressure, particularly from the United States and the Soviet Union, ultimately compelled
the invading forces to withdraw. Today, it is managed by the Suez Canal Authority and
generates billions of dollars annually for Egypt.
Despite its robust economic contributions, the Suez Canal faces ongoing challenges that
threaten its operational stability and long-term viability. Periodic blockages, such as the
infamous 2021 incident involving the grounding of the container ship Ever Given, highlight
the canal’s vulnerability to disruptions. Such blockages can have cascading effects on
global supply chains, leading to delays, increased shipping costs, and economic losses for
businesses worldwide.

Extract A: Sea Safety - Letter to the editor
Once again another sea rescue that was completely unnecessary has taken place. Small
craft, sailing vessels and helicopters have been involved in a four-day search of our
coastline, often in appalling weather and dangerous seas because of human stupidity.
| am very pleased that the Haslan family was finally rescued from the serious danger they
were in, but the danger was of their own making. Reports indicate that the minimum safety
requirement and safety kits were not on board. Not to have the correct safety equipment,
sufficient safety floatation devices and communicating equipment and setting off past
Barr's Point into the open sea, can only be described as almost criminal negligence.
The weather forecast on the morning the family set out indicated rising seas and steadily
increasing winds, though only freshening during the afternoon to 17 - 21 knots. The area
outside Barr's Point is well known as a place where the current can run in the opposite
direction to the waves. When this happens the waves can overrun each other and this in
turn generates steep and dangerous rogue waves. In this part of the world, the weather
forecasts for fishermen and the general conditions north and south of Eastview are well
known, widely advertised and most people take the necessary precautions to ensure the
safety of the lives of their family.
What did this rescue cost in terms of official police, rescue personnel and volunteers? A
large sum of money no doubt. It is time people who, through their own ignorance, lack of
responsibility and common sense, were made to pay to our local council at least part of the
overall cost of their rescue.
Extract B: Excerpt from ‘The Coral Island: A Tale of the Pacific Ocean’ by R.M.
Ballantyne
| shall say little about the first part of our voyage. We had the usual amount of rough
weather and calm; also we saw many strange fish rolling in the sea, and | was greatly
delighted one day by seeing a shoal of flying fish dart out of the water and skim through
the air about a foot above the surface. They were pursued by dolphins, which feed on
them, and one flying-fish in its terror flew over the ship, struck on the rigging, and fell upon
the deck. Its wings were just fins elongated, and we found that they could never fly far at a
time, and never mounted into the air like birds, but skimmed along the surface of the sea.
Jack and | had it for dinner, and found it remarkably good.
When we approached Cape Horn, at the southern extremity of America, the weather
became very cold and stormy, and the sailors began to tell stories about the furious gales
and the dangers of that terrible cape. Each story outdid the one before in conjuring fearful
possibilities.
Nevertheless, we passed the dreaded cape without much rough weather, and, in the
course of a few weeks afterwards, were sailing gently, before a warm tropical breeze, over
the Pacific Ocean. Thus we proceeded on our voyage, sometimes bounding merrily before
a fair breeze, at other times floating calmly on the glassy wave and fishing for the curious
inhabitants of the deep - all of which, although the sailors thought little of them, were
strange, and interesting, and very wonderful to me.

Good Timber
by Douglas Malloch
The tree that never had to fight
For sun and sky and air and light,
But stood out in the open plain
And always got its share of rain,
Never became a forest king
But lived and died a scrubby thing.
The man who never had to toil
To gain and farm his patch of soil,
Who never had to win his share
Of sun and sky and light and air,
Never became a manly man
But lived and died as he began.
Good timber does not grow with ease,
The stronger wind, the stronger trees,
The further sky, the greater length,
The more the storm, the more the strength.
By sun and cold, by rain and snow,
In trees and men good timbers grow.
Where thickest lies the forest growth
We find the patriarchs of both.
And they hold counsel with the stars
Whose broken branches show the scars
Of many winds and much of strife.
This is the common law of life.

Extract A: Excerpt from ‘To Kill a Mockingbird’ By Harper Lee
Our father didn’t do anything. He worked in an office, not in a drugstore. Atticus did not
drive a dump-truck for the country, he was not the sheriff, he did not farm, work in a
garage, or do anything that could possibly arouse the admiration of anyone.
Besides that, he wore glasses. He was nearly blind in his left eye, and said left eyes were
the tribal curse of the Finches. Whenever he wanted to see something well, he turned his
head and looked from his right eye. He did not do the things our schoolmates’ fathers did:
he never went hunting, he did not play poker or fish or drink or smoke. He sat in the living
room and read.
With these attributes, however, he would not remain as inconspicuous as we wished him
to: that year, the school buzzed with talk about him defending Tom Robinson, none of
which was complimentary. After my bout with Cecil Jacobs when | committed myself to a
policy of cowardice, word got around that Scout Finch wouldn’t fight any more, her daddy
wouldn't let her. This was not entirely correct: | wouldn't fight publicly for Atticus, but the
family was private ground. | would fight anyone from a third cousin upwards tooth and nail.
Francis Hancock, for example, knew that.
When he gave us our air-rifles Atticus wouldn’t teach us to shoot. Uncle Jack instructed us
in the rudiments thereof; he said Atticus wasn’t interested in guns. Atticus said to Jem one
day, “I'd rather you shot at tin cans in the back yard, but | know you'll go after birds. Shoot
all the bluejays you want, if you can hit ‘em, but remember it’s a sin to kill a mockingbird.”
That was the only time | ever heard Atticus say it was a sin to do something, and | asked
Miss Maudie about it. “Your father’s right,” she said. “Mockingbirds don’t do one thing but

My dear father had been killed by the Doones of Bagworthy, while riding home from
Porlock market, on the Saturday evening. With him were six brother-farmers, all of them
very sober; for father would have no company with any man who went beyond half a
gallon of beer, or a single gallon of cider. The robbers had no grudge against him; for he

By dress and arms they knew him well, and by his size and stature, shown against the

his staff above his head, and rode at the Doone robber. With a trick of his horse, the wild
man escaped the sudden onset, although it must have amazed him sadly that anyone

| wandered across the vast desert, where the burning sun left the earth both harsh and
strangely beautiful. In that quiet, endless expanse, each parched stone and withering
wildflower whispered a secret of resilience—a silent testimony to nature’s unyielding spirit.
As | ambled along the sun-cracked path, the arid wind carried with it a tapestry of dust and
distant memories, reminding me that even the most barren lands possess their own subtle,
poetic grace.
The desert, with its scorching days and chilly nights, was not merely a wasteland but a
living canvas painted with the shifting hues of time. Each ripple in the sand seemed to
echo the footsteps of those who had traversed this unforgiving terrain long before me. The
sparse vegetation, clinging stubbornly to life in crevices -and along weathered rock faces,
told stories of survival against overwhelming odds. | paused before a solitary shrub, its
gnarled branches silhouetted against a molten sky, and felt a kinship with its silent
struggle—a reflection of humanity’s own persistent quest to find meaning in desolation.
In that moment, the desert transformed before my eyes. What once appeared as a stark
and lifeless void revealed itself to be a mosaic of wonder, where every grain of sand was a
piece of an ancient puzzle and every breeze carried whispers of forgotten lore. The subtle
interplay of light and shadow danced across the dunes, as if nature herself were
composing a quiet symphony of renewal. The heat, while oppressive, also nurtured a
unique form of beauty, one that was raw and unfiltered—a beauty that demanded
reverence and care.
! found myself drawn deeper into the landscape, compelled to explore not only the physical
vastness but the inner wilderness that it stirred within me. The desert was a mirror
reflecting the delicate balance between destruction and creation. Here, in this realm of
extremes, the human spirit could learn the art of letting go—of releasing the weight of
modern expectations and embracing a simpler, more authentic connection with the land.
This pilgrimage through the desert awakened in me an acute awareness of our shared
responsibility. Just as the resilient wildflower fought against the odds to bloom in the arid
soil, so too must we nurture our own fragile ecosystems against the encroachment of
neglect and exploitation. The landscape, etched by both the scars of human activity and
the enduring pulse of nature, called out for protection—a plea for us to remember that the

Extract B: Excerpt from ‘To protect New Yorkers from floods and droughts, protect
wetlands‘ by Pete Lopez and Alex Wolf
For centuries, wetlands were often viewed as swamps or waste grounds, land to be
‘improved’ by draining and clearing. Although draining wetlands resulted in productive
farmland in some areas, it also came with a price — one that grows costlier over time.
Wetlands, including marshes, swamps, bogs and vernal pools, are critical to absorbing
rainwater. As we experience increasingly severe storms, our lack of wetlands is hitting
home harder every year. Where wetlands remain, they help filter pollutants, control the
flow of water into our streams and rivers, and reduce storm surge impacts.
Recognising the importance of wetlands, new statewide protections went into effect on
Jan. 1 as amendments to New York’s Freshwater Wetlands Act, first enacted 50 years ago.
Importantly, the new amendments provide for higher levels of wetland protection in flood
zones recognised by the Federal Emergency Management Agency. They also focus on
wetlands in urban areas and those vital for drinking water, wildlife and recreation.
In places where we’ve replaced wetlands with drainage canals, ditches or pavement, the
water races along at high speed, overfilling our creeks, slamming into bridges and washing
away roads. In more populated areas, it gushes along streets and traps people in homes
and cars.
During Superstorm Sandy in 2012, coastal wetlands prevented nearly $1 million dollars of
damage in the Rockland County village of Piermont alone, and $625 million in damages
across the region. Those savings multiply across the state over many years and many
storms.
Wetlands are also crucial to combatting drought and wildfires, a fact that came into the
spotlight during last summer’s unprecedented Hudson Valley wildfires. Wetlands help
recharge our water supplies for the drier months. Floods and drought are opposite sides of
the coin. Wetlands help with both issues.
